questions.stem: The ratio of COD to BOD of untreated sewage is:
questions.solution:
**1.25 to 1.5.**

The two demands measure overlapping but unequal things:

| | Measures | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **BOD** | Oxygen to oxidise the **biodegradable** organics only | Biological, 5 days at 20°C |
| **COD** | Oxygen to oxidise **biodegradable *and* non-biodegradable** organics | Chemical, about 3 hours |

Because COD captures everything BOD captures **plus** the refractory fraction, **COD is always greater than BOD**, and the ratio is always above 1.

For **untreated domestic sewage** the organic load is largely biodegradable, so the two figures are close and the ratio sits at about **1.25 to 1.5**.

The ratio is diagnostic, which is why it is examined:
- **BOD/COD > 0.5** — readily biodegradable, so biological treatment (activated sludge, trickling filter) will work. Domestic sewage sits here.
- **BOD/COD < 0.3** — largely refractory, typical of industrial effluent; needs chemical or advanced treatment instead.

Note that the ratio **widens after treatment**: a biological plant removes the biodegradable fraction preferentially, so the effluent has proportionally more refractory matter and a higher COD/BOD ratio than the raw sewage.

examTip.trick: **COD is ALWAYS greater than BOD** — chemical oxidation attacks everything, while biological oxidation reaches only the biodegradable fraction. So the ratio must exceed 1, which kills any option below it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Domestic sewage 1.25–1.5; industrial effluent much higher** (2–5 or more, because of non-biodegradable organics). A **rising COD/BOD ratio is itself a warning** that industrial waste is entering a domestic sewer.

questions.stem: The slenderness ratio (S/d) of a solid circular timber column should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**50.**

For a solid timber column the slenderness ratio is the unsupported length divided by the least lateral dimension — for a circular section, the diameter. IS 883 caps it at **50** for a solid column.

Beyond that limit the column becomes so slender that buckling governs completely and the section can no longer be relied on: small accidental eccentricities and the natural variability of timber make the behaviour unpredictable.

The timber column limits worth carrying:

| Member | Limit on S/d |
|---|---|
| **Solid column** | **50** |
| Built-up / box column | 80 |
| Compression member carrying wind load only | 80 |

Timber columns are classified by the same ratio:

| Class | S/d | Governing behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Short | < 11 | Crushing |
| Intermediate | 11 – 30 | Combined |
| Long | > 30 | Buckling (Euler) |

Compare the limits in other materials, since the numbers are easily mixed up: IS 456 caps the **unsupported length of an RCC column** at 60 times its least lateral dimension, and IS 800 limits the slenderness ratio (l/r, using the radius of gyration rather than the dimension) to **180** for a member carrying compression from dead and live load.

examTip.trick: Timber's slenderness is checked on **S/d** (length over least dimension), not on L/r as for steel. Solid columns are limited to **50**, and box or built-up columns to 40.
examTip.mnemonic: **Timber 50, and it is checked on the LEAST lateral dimension.** Beyond that limit the column is treated as unusable rather than merely derated — timber's variability makes very slender members unreliable.

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a hemisphere is at:
questions.solution:
**3r/8 from the base.**

For a solid hemisphere of radius r, integrating the elemental discs gives the centroid at

> ȳ = **3r/8** measured from the flat circular face

The centroids that get confused with one another — commit the whole set, because examiners rotate through them:

| Shape | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8 from base** |
| Hemispherical shell (surface) | r/2 from base |
| Solid cone | h/4 from base |
| Semicircular **area** (lamina) | 4r/3π from base |
| Semicircular **arc** (wire) | 2r/π from base |
| Triangle | h/3 from base |

Option (d), 4r/3π, is the standard trap: that is the centroid of a **semicircular lamina** — a two-dimensional area — not of a three-dimensional hemisphere.

A quick sanity check that rules out most wrong options: the centroid of a solid hemisphere must lie **below** the mid-height r/2, because more material sits near the flat base than near the pole. And 3r/8 = 0.375r is indeed less than 0.5r ✓ while 3r/4 = 0.75r is not.

examTip.trap: **r/2** is the value for a **HOLLOW** hemisphere and is the standard confusion. Also distinct is **4r/3π** for a semicircular **area** — a two-dimensional figure.
examTip.trick: A solid hemisphere has more material near its flat base, so its centroid must sit **lower** than the shell's: **3r/8 = 0.375r < 0.5r** ✓ — the inequality alone identifies it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid 3r/8, hollow r/2, semicircular area 4r/3π, semicircular arc 2r/π.** Four values, four different figures.

questions.stem: The Froude number of a triangular channel of depth y with side slope 2H : 1V is:
questions.solution:
**V / √(g · y/2).**

The Froude number for any open channel uses the **hydraulic depth** D, not the flow depth y:

> Fr = V / √(gD),  where **D = A / T** (area ÷ top width)

**For the triangular section with side slope 2H : 1V:**
Each side extends 2y horizontally for a depth y, so with both sides sloping,
> T = 2 × 2y = 4y
> A = ½ × T × y = ½ × 4y × y = 2y²
> **D = A/T = 2y²/4y = y/2**

> **Fr = V / √(g·y/2)** ✓

Note that D = y/2 for *any* triangular channel, whatever the side slope — the slope cancels between area and top width. That is worth remembering as a standing result.

**Contrast with a rectangular channel:**
> A = by, T = b, so D = by/b = **y**, and Fr = V/√(gy)

which is where option (c) comes from — it is the rectangular-channel answer.

The interpretation: **Fr < 1** subcritical (deep, slow, gravity dominant), **Fr = 1** critical, **Fr > 1** supercritical (shallow, fast). A hydraulic jump can only form when the upstream flow is supercritical.

examTip.trick: The general Froude number is **V/√(gD)** where **D = A/T** is the **hydraulic depth**, not the maximum depth. For a triangle, A = zy² and T = 2zy, so **D = y/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr uses A/T, the HYDRAULIC depth.** For a wide rectangular channel A/T = y, which is why the simple V/√(gy) form works there — and why it fails for a triangle or a trapezoid.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the stream length of fan shaped and fern shaped catchments?
options: Stream length of fan shaped catchment is more
Stream length of fern shaped catchment is more
Stream length of both catchments is same
questions.solution:
**The fern shaped catchment has the greater stream length.**

The two shapes behave quite differently, and the contrast is what gets examined:

| | **Fan shaped** | **Fern shaped** |
|---|---|---|
| Plan shape | Broad, roughly circular or semicircular | **Elongated, narrow, leaf-like** |
| Main stream length | Shorter | **Longer** |
| Tributaries | Short, joining near the outlet | Long, joining along the length |
| Time of concentration | **Short** | **Long** |
| Flood hydrograph | **High, sharp peak** | Low, flat, drawn-out peak |

In a **fern shaped** catchment the water must travel a long way down an elongated basin before reaching the outlet, so the flow path — and hence the stream length — is greater.

The hydrological consequence matters more than the geometry. In a **fan shaped** catchment, run-off from all parts of the basin arrives at the outlet at roughly the same time, so the contributions **superimpose** and produce a sharp, dangerous flood peak. In a fern shaped catchment the arrivals are staggered over a long period, so the peak is attenuated even though the total volume may be the same.

That is why catchment shape enters flood estimation through the **form factor** (A/L²) and the **compactness coefficient**, and why a fan shaped catchment of a given area needs a larger design discharge than a fern shaped one.

examTip.trick: Catchment **shape** controls the hydrograph. A **fan-shaped** catchment delivers all its tributaries to the outlet at once, giving a **high, early peak**. A **fern-shaped (elongated)** one has a longer main stream and staggered arrivals, giving a **lower, later, broader** peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fan = flashy; fern = flat.** The quantitative measure is the **form factor** (A/L²) or the **compactness coefficient** — and the difference in peak discharge between the two shapes can be a factor of two.

questions.stem: Blue baby syndrome is caused due to:
questions.solution:
**Nitrate.**

Blue baby syndrome — clinically **methaemoglobinaemia** — is caused by excess **nitrate (NO₃⁻)** in drinking water. In an infant's gut, bacteria reduce the nitrate to nitrite, which oxidises the iron in haemoglobin to form **methaemoglobin**. Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity falls and the baby takes on a bluish tinge.

Infants under six months are especially vulnerable because their stomach is less acidic (so the reducing bacteria thrive) and their foetal haemoglobin is more readily oxidised.

**Permissible limit: 50 mg/L as NO₃⁻**, or 10 mg/L expressed as nitrate-nitrogen.

Usual sources of nitrate in groundwater: **agricultural fertiliser leaching**, septic tank and latrine seepage, and animal waste — which is why shallow wells near latrines are a particular concern in rural Nepal.

The other water-quality parameters and the problems they cause, a standard exam pairing:

| Constituent | Effect | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Nitrate** | **Blue baby syndrome** | 50 mg/L |
| Fluoride | Deficiency → dental caries; excess → **fluorosis** | 0.5–1.5 mg/L |
| Arsenic | Skin lesions, cancer — a serious problem in the Terai | 0.01 mg/L (WHO); 0.05 mg/L (Nepal interim) |
| Iron | Taste, staining of fixtures and laundry | 0.3 mg/L |
| Chloride | Salty taste | 250 mg/L |
| Sulphate | Laxative effect | 250 mg/L |

Note the distinction the options are probing: nitrite is the *agent* formed inside the body, but **nitrate** is the contaminant present in the water and is the answer to what causes the condition.

examTip.trick: **Methaemoglobinaemia** — nitrate is reduced to nitrite in an infant's gut, which converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport, turning the skin blue.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nitrate → blue baby. Fluoride → fluorosis (mottled teeth above 1.5 mg/l, skeletal above 3). Arsenic → skin lesions and cancer.** Arsenic is the serious groundwater problem in Nepal's **Terai**, with a national standard of 50 µg/l against the WHO's 10.

questions.stem: A train of wheel loads is moving over a simply supported beam. The shear force will be maximum at support A when:
options: Shear force will be equal in all cases
questions.solution:
**When the trailing load is at A.**

The influence line for shear force at support A of a simply supported beam has its **maximum ordinate at A itself** and falls linearly to zero at the far support B. To maximise the shear, the loads must therefore be positioned so that as much of the train as possible sits over the high-ordinate region near A — while **all** the loads remain on the span.

If the **leading** load is placed at A, the rest of the train trails off the beam and contributes nothing. If instead the **trailing** (last) load is brought up to A, the whole train is on the span and packed as close to A as it can be, so every wheel contributes its load times a positive influence ordinate.

That gives the greatest sum, so the trailing load at A governs.

The companion results for a moving train on a simply supported span, which are examined together:

| Quantity | Position for maximum |
|---|---|
| **Shear at a support** | **Trailing load at that support**, whole train on span |
| Shear at a section | Load just to one side of the section |
| **Bending moment** | **Under one of the wheel loads** (never mid-span for a train) |
| Absolute maximum BM | Under the load nearest the resultant, positioned near mid-span |

Recall from Set 1 Q5 that the maximum bending moment always occurs **under a wheel load**, because the BM diagram is piecewise linear and can only peak at a break point.

examTip.trick: For maximum **shear at a section**, the influence line is two parallel lines with a unit step. You want the loads massed over the **larger-ordinate** side — so the train is positioned with a load right at the section and the rest on the heavier side.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum shear at a support: put the LEADING load at the support and the rest on the span.** Maximum shear at an interior section: load one side only, because the influence line changes sign and loading both partly cancels.

questions.stem: The gross area of a footing is dependent on:
questions.solution:
**All of these.**

The governing relation is simply

> Area required = Total load / Safe bearing capacity

and every option feeds into one side of that equation:

- **Load from the superstructure** is the numerator — dead plus live load, plus the self-weight of the footing and the earth over it.
- **Bearing capacity of the soil** is the denominator, so the area is inversely proportional to it. A weak soil demands a large footing for the same load.
- **Type of soil** determines that bearing capacity in the first place, through c, φ and γ, and also decides which criterion governs. In **sand** the strength criterion usually governs; in **clay** the settlement criterion usually governs and forces a larger area than strength alone would require.

Since all three enter the calculation, (d) is the answer.

The design sequence in practice:
1. Compute the safe bearing capacity, q_{safe} = q_{nu}/FoS + γD_{f}, with FoS of 2.5 to 3.
2. Check the **allowable** bearing pressure, which is the lesser of q_{safe} and the pressure that keeps settlement within permissible limits.
3. Area = total service load ÷ allowable bearing pressure.
4. Proportion the plan so the pressure is as uniform as possible, then design the section for **bending, one-way shear and two-way (punching) shear**.

Note the distinction the wording invites: the **gross** area carries the total load including the footing's own weight and the backfill above it, whereas the **net** area relates only to the load in excess of the overburden that was there before.

examTip.trap: "All of these" rewards reading every option — the gross area depends on the load, the allowable pressure and the depth, all at once.
examTip.trick: **A = total service load / net allowable bearing pressure**, and the **net** pressure depends on the depth through γD_f. So depth enters as well as load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Area from SERVICE loads and the net allowable pressure; structural design from FACTORED loads.** Mixing the two double-counts the safety factor and doubles the footing.

questions.stem: The depth of exploration is independent of:
questions.solution:
**Type of boring.**

The depth to which a site must be explored is decided by **how deep the structure's influence reaches into the ground** — not by the equipment used to make the hole. Auger boring, wash boring, percussion or rotary drilling are simply alternative *means* of reaching a required depth; the method is chosen to suit the soil and the depth, so it is a consequence of the requirement rather than a determinant of it.

Why each of the others does matter:
- **Size of structure** — the significant stress zone scales with the footing width. IS 1892 requires exploration to at least **1.5 B** below an isolated square footing and about **3 B** below a strip footing, so a bigger footing needs a deeper hole.
- **Load of structure** — a heavier load spreads its influence deeper before the added stress becomes negligible.
- **Type of structure** — a raft, a pile group and isolated footings transmit load quite differently, and a pile foundation must be explored well below the anticipated toe level.

The usual rule of thumb: explore until the **net added vertical stress falls to about 10% of the applied pressure**, or to 20% of the *in situ* overburden pressure, whichever is shallower — and always down to bedrock where that is within reach.

**A note on the source explanation.** The circulating answer sheet keys (c), which is right, but the paragraph beneath it argues that "the type of structure does not directly affect the depth of exploration" — reasoning towards (b). That reasoning is wrong: IS 1892 explicitly varies the required depth with the type of foundation. The keyed letter is correct; the explanation has been rewritten.

verification.notes: The keyed letter (c) is correct, but the source's own explanation argues for (b), claiming the type of structure does not affect exploration depth. IS 1892 varies required depth with foundation type, so that reasoning is wrong. The explanation has been rewritten while keeping the correct answer.

examTip.trick: Depth of exploration follows the **stress bulb** — the load, the footing width and the soil profile. **How** you make the hole (auger, wash boring, rotary) is a matter of technique and has nothing to do with how deep you need to go.
examTip.mnemonic: **Explore to 1.5–2 B below the footing**, and for a **pile group** measure from the pile TIPS, not from ground level. For a large raft, B is the whole raft width — which can mean very deep boreholes.

questions.stem: In a simply supported beam of span L, two equal point loads P are acting at a distance of L/3 from both supports A and B. What is the value of shear force at a distance L/6 from support A?
questions.solution:
**P.**

**Step 1 — reactions.** The loading is symmetric, so each support carries half the total:
> R_{A} = R_{B} = 2P/2 = **P**

**Step 2 — shear at L/6 from A.** The section at L/6 lies **between support A and the first load** (which sits at L/3). Taking forces to the left of the section, only R_{A} is present:
> V = R_{A} = **P**

**Why the answer does not change across that whole region.** Between A and the first load there is no intervening force, so the shear force is **constant at P** everywhere from x = 0 to x = L/3. The section at L/6 is simply one point in that constant region — the L/6 in the question is a distractor, not a quantity you need.

The complete shear force diagram, worth sketching mentally:

| Region | Shear force |
|---|---|
| 0 to L/3 | **+P** |
| L/3 to 2L/3 | **0** |
| 2L/3 to L | **−P** |

The zero-shear middle third is the significant feature: since V = dM/dx, zero shear means the bending moment is **constant** there, at M = P·L/3. That is the classic condition of **pure bending**, and it is exactly why this two-point loading arrangement is used in the standard **flexure test** on beams and in four-point bending tests — the middle third experiences uniform moment with no shear.

examTip.trick: With two equal loads P placed symmetrically, each reaction is **P**, and between the loads the shear is **zero** while the moment is **constant** — a region of **pure bending**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two symmetric point loads create PURE BENDING between them** — constant moment, zero shear. That is exactly why the **four-point (third-point) loading test** is used for flexural strength: it gives a length of beam in uniform moment, uncontaminated by shear.

questions.stem: What is the value of excess pressure inside a soap bubble having radius R?
questions.solution:
**4T/R.**

A soap bubble is a thin film with **two** surfaces in contact with air — an inner and an outer. Each surface contributes a surface-tension force, so the excess pressure is twice that of a single-surface droplet:

> Δp = **4T/R** = 8T/D

**Derivation.** Balancing forces on a hemisphere of the bubble: pressure force outward = Δp × πR², surface tension force inward = T × 2 × (2πR) — the factor 2 for the two surfaces. Equating:
> Δp × πR² = 4πRT ⟹ Δp = 4T/R ✓

The three standard results, distinguished by geometry and by the number of surfaces:

| Case | Surfaces | In terms of R | In terms of D |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liquid **droplet** | 1 | 2T/R | 4T/D |
| **Soap bubble** | **2** | **4T/R** | **8T/D** |
| Liquid **jet** (cylinder) | 1 | T/R | 2T/D |

Be careful which variable the question uses — this is the single commonest error here. **4T/R and 8T/D are the same quantity**; Set 1 Q78 of this series quoted the bubble result as 8σ/d, using diameter. Read whether the question gives radius or diameter before choosing.

Since Δp ∝ 1/R, a **smaller bubble has a higher internal pressure**, which is why two connected bubbles of unequal size end with the small one emptying into the large one.

examTip.trick: In terms of **radius**: **Δp = 4T/R** for a soap bubble. In terms of **diameter** the same thing reads **8T/d**. Both are correct — check which the question uses.
examTip.mnemonic: **Radius form: droplet 2T/R, bubble 4T/R, jet T/R. Diameter form: 4T/d, 8T/d, 2T/d.** Mixing the two conventions is the trap here, and it costs a factor of two.

questions.stem: The flow duration curve at a given head of a hydroelectric plant is used to determine:
options: Total power available at the site
questions.solution:
**Total power available at the site.**

A **flow duration curve** plots discharge against the percentage of time that discharge is equalled or exceeded, built by ranking the historical flow record. It is a statement about the **water resource**, not about the electrical demand.

Since power at a fixed head is P = ηγQH, each discharge on the curve converts directly into a power ordinate. So at a given head the flow duration curve becomes a **power duration curve**, and from it the engineer reads off the power available for any chosen reliability — for example the flow available 90% of the time (Q₉₀), which fixes the **firm or dependable power** of the scheme.

Why the other options are wrong:
- **Total units of energy** requires the **area under** the curve, not the curve read directly. Energy is power integrated over time, so this is a derived quantity — the distinction the question is testing.
- **Load factor** and **diversity factor** are properties of the **electrical demand**, obtained from the load curve and the consumers' usage pattern. A flow duration curve carries no information about them at all.

The closely related curves, frequently confused:

| Curve | Plots | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Flow duration** | Discharge vs % time exceeded | **Available power; firm power** |
| Mass (Rippl) curve | Cumulative inflow vs time | **Reservoir storage capacity** |
| Load curve | Demand vs time of day | Peak demand, load factor |
| Load duration curve | Demand vs % time exceeded | Plant capacity mix |

A **steep** flow duration curve indicates a flashy, variable river with little dependable flow; a **flat** one indicates well-sustained flow, often from snowmelt or good baseflow, and gives a much higher firm power for the same mean discharge.

examTip.trick: A flow duration curve plots discharge against the **percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded**. Combined with the head it gives the **power available for each proportion of the year** — which is the basis of a hydropower yield study.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q₄₀ is the flow exceeded 40% of the time**, and it is the conventional design flow for a run-of-river scheme in Nepal. The curve's **flatness** matters as much as its height: a flat curve means dependable flow, a steep one means a flashy river with little dry-season yield.

questions.stem: What is the standard temperature for the Marshall Stability test?
questions.solution:
**60°C.**

The Marshall test measures the resistance of a compacted bituminous mix to deformation. It is conducted at **60°C** because that approximates the **hottest pavement surface temperature** reached in service — the condition in which a bituminous mix is weakest and most liable to rut. Testing at room temperature would flatter the mix and tell the designer nothing useful.

Procedure in outline: a cylindrical specimen 101.6 mm diameter × 63.5 mm high is compacted with **75 blows per face** for heavy traffic, immersed in a water bath at **60°C for 30 to 40 minutes**, then loaded diametrally at **50.8 mm/minute** until failure.

Two results are read:
- **Marshall stability** — the peak load in kN. Minimum about **9 kN** for heavy traffic.
- **Flow value** — the deformation at peak load, in units of 0.25 mm. Acceptable range about **8 to 16**.

The design bitumen content is chosen from plots of stability, flow, unit weight, air voids and voids filled with bitumen against binder content, and is the value that satisfies all the specified limits simultaneously — commonly around 5%.

Do not confuse this 60°C with the temperatures of the other bitumen tests, all of which appear as distractors here:

| Test | Standard temperature |
|---|---|
| **Marshall stability** | **60°C** |
| **Penetration** | **25°C** (100 g, 5 s) |
| Ductility | 27°C |
| Softening point (ring and ball) | Measured, typically 35–70°C |
| Viscosity (bitumen) | 60°C or 135°C |

examTip.trick: **60 °C** is chosen to represent the **hottest pavement temperature** a bituminous surface actually reaches in service — the condition in which it is most likely to deform.
examTip.mnemonic: **Marshall: 60 °C, 75 blows per face for heavy traffic.** The test yields **stability** (load at failure) and **flow** (deformation) — and the design bitumen content is chosen from a set of curves, not from stability alone.

questions.stem: Due to a lined channel section:
questions.solution:
**Command area increases.**

Lining a canal with concrete, brick or a membrane cuts **seepage loss** dramatically — typically by 60 to 80%. That saved water stays in the canal and can be delivered to fields, so the same headworks discharge now irrigates a **larger command area**. This is the principal justification for the expense of lining.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Waterlogging decreases**, not increases. Seepage from unlined canals is one of the main causes of a rising water table in a command area; lining removes that source. Option (a) has the sign backwards.
- **Cross-sectional area decreases** for the same discharge. A lined surface is much smoother — Manning's n falls from about 0.025 in earth to 0.015 in concrete — so the velocity is higher and a **smaller** section carries the same Q. That saves land and earthwork.

The full set of benefits, which is what the question is really probing:

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Larger command area** | Seepage saved becomes usable water |
| Reduced waterlogging and salinity | Water table no longer fed by canal seepage |
| Smaller section, less land | Lower n, higher permissible velocity |
| No silting or scouring | Stable, non-erodible boundary |
| Lower maintenance | Weed growth and berm cutting largely eliminated |
| Safety against breach | Banks not weakened by saturation |

Against these: high initial cost, difficulty of repair, and loss of the groundwater recharge that seepage previously provided — which is why lining is justified by a **benefit–cost analysis**, as in Set 1 Q68.

examTip.trick: Lining does three things at once, and all of them increase the area that can be served: it **stops seepage losses**, permits a **higher velocity** (hence a smaller section), and **prevents weed growth**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Less water lost = more land irrigated from the same headworks.** Lining also removes the **waterlogging** that canal seepage causes in adjacent fields — often the decisive benefit, because waterlogging brings salinity with it.

questions.stem: Water is flowing down steadily in a constant cross-sectional pipe. According to Bernoulli's principle:
questions.solution:
**Pressure decreases with height.**

Bernoulli's equation along the pipe:

> p/γ + v²/2g + z = constant

**Step 1 — the velocity term is fixed.** The pipe has a **constant cross-section** and the flow is steady, so by continuity Q = Av gives v = constant throughout. The velocity head v²/2g therefore drops out of the comparison entirely — which also disposes of option (c).

**Step 2 — pressure and elevation must trade off.** With the velocity head constant, the equation reduces to
> p/γ + z = constant

So as the elevation z **increases**, the pressure head p/γ must **decrease** by exactly the same amount.

That is the answer, and it is also just the familiar hydrostatic result: higher up the pipe, there is less water above you, so the pressure is lower. At the bottom of a penstock the pressure is enormous; at the intake it is small.

**A caution on the wording.** "Flowing down" describes the direction of travel; the question asks how pressure varies **with height**, which is a spatial comparison. As the water flows *downward* it moves to lower z, so the pressure it experiences **rises** — the same physical fact stated the other way round. Read carefully which way the comparison runs.

In a real pipe there is also friction, so the total head falls in the flow direction:
> p₁/γ + v₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/γ + v₂²/2g + z₂ + h_{L}

but the qualitative conclusion about pressure and height is unchanged.

examTip.trick: In a **constant cross-section** pipe the velocity cannot change (continuity), so the velocity head is fixed. Bernoulli then requires that as **elevation falls, pressure rises** — so going **up**, pressure decreases.
examTip.mnemonic: **Constant area means constant velocity, so pressure trades purely against elevation** — exactly as in a static fluid. It is only where the section changes that the velocity head enters the exchange.

questions.stem: A solid having an equilateral triangle as base and other faces converging towards its axis is:
questions.solution:
**Pyramid.**

The defining feature in the question is that the side faces **converge to a point** on the axis. That is precisely a pyramid: a polygonal base with triangular faces meeting at a single apex. With an equilateral triangle as the base it is a **triangular pyramid**, also called a tetrahedron when all four faces are equilateral.

Why the others fail:

| Solid | Faces | Converge? |
|---|---|---|
| **Prism** | Two identical **parallel** bases joined by rectangles | **No** — sides are parallel |
| **Pyramid** | One polygonal base, triangular sides to an **apex** | **Yes** |
| **Hexahedron** | Six faces — a cube is the regular case | No |
| **Cone** | **Circular** base, curved surface to an apex | Yes, but the base is not a polygon |

So the cone is the near miss: it converges to an apex but requires a *circular* base, whereas the question specifies an equilateral triangle. A cone is in effect the limiting case of a pyramid as the number of base sides tends to infinity.

For mensuration, the volume rule is common to both converging solids and is worth carrying:

> Volume of pyramid or cone = **⅓ × base area × height**
> Volume of prism or cylinder = base area × height

So a pyramid holds exactly one third of the prism that shares its base and height. Its lateral surface area is ½ × perimeter of base × **slant height**.

examTip.trick: **Pyramid**: a polygonal base with triangular faces meeting at an apex. A **prism** has two parallel identical faces; a **cone** has a circular base; a **tetrahedron** is the special case of a pyramid with a triangular base and three faces.
examTip.mnemonic: **Base shape names the pyramid** — triangular base gives a triangular pyramid (a tetrahedron if all four faces are equilateral).

questions.stem: Which method gives accurate flow characteristics in the context of rivers of Nepal?
questions.solution:
**DHM 2004.**

Nepal has very few gauged catchments relative to the number of schemes needing design flows, so discharge at an ungauged site is estimated by **regional regression methods** calibrated on the gauged record. Three generations of such methods are in circulation, and the question asks which is the most accurate:

| Method | Origin | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **MIP (1982)** | Medium Irrigation Project | Earliest; regional monthly flow coefficients from a short record |
| **WECS/DHM (1990)** | Water and Energy Commission Secretariat with DHM | Regression on catchment area **below 5000 m** elevation, plus monsoon rainfall |
| **DHM (2004)** | *Hydrological Estimations in Nepal*, DHM | Latest; longer and denser gauge record, refined regionalisation |

**DHM 2004** is built on a substantially longer and better-distributed streamflow record than the two earlier studies, with improved regional grouping, so it gives the most reliable estimates and supersedes them for new work.

The **WECS/DHM 1990** method remains the most widely *used* in practice — many feasibility studies still quote it, and its distinctive feature is that it uses only the catchment area lying **below 5000 m**, on the reasoning that the perpetually snow-covered area above that contributes little to the monsoon flood.

A point worth carrying for design: whichever regional method is used, the estimate should be checked against any nearby gauged record by **catchment area ratio transposition**, and against a rainfall–runoff estimate, because regional regressions carry wide confidence bands on individual catchments.

examTip.trick: For **ungauged** catchments — which is most of Nepal — regional methods derived from the country's own gauged records are far more reliable than formulae transplanted from elsewhere.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use regional methods calibrated on LOCAL data.** The general principle behind it: where a long **gauged record exists, frequency analysis always beats any rainfall-based estimate**, because it uses the catchment's observed behaviour rather than a chain of assumptions.

questions.stem: Lacquer is:
questions.solution:
**A spirit varnish.**

Lacquer is a resin dissolved in a **volatile spirit solvent**, usually alcohol or a similar fast-evaporating thinner. It dries purely by **evaporation** of that solvent, leaving a hard, clear or pigmented film — so it dries very fast, but the film stays comparatively brittle and is attacked by the same solvent that carried it.

That evaporative mechanism is the key: it makes lacquer a **spirit varnish**, distinct from paints that dry by oxidation or by chemical curing.

The four classes of finish the options draw on:

| Finish | Vehicle | Dries by | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lacquer (spirit varnish)** | **Volatile spirit** | **Evaporation** | Wood, furniture, brass fittings |
| Oil varnish | Drying oil + resin | Oxidation | Exterior joinery — slower, tougher, more durable |
| Oil paint | Linseed oil + pigment | Oxidation | General exterior and interior work |
| Distemper | **Water** + chalk + glue | Evaporation of water | Cheap interior wall finish; not washable |
| Enamel paint | Oil or alkyd resin | Oxidation / curing | Hard, glossy, washable — kitchens, bathrooms, steelwork |

So distemper is the water-based cheap wall finish, enamel the hard glossy alkyd, and lacquer the fast-drying spirit finish for woodwork.

The types of varnish are a related exam list: **spirit varnish** (lacquer), **oil varnish** (durable, exterior), **turpentine varnish**, **water varnish** and **flat varnish**.

examTip.trick: Varnishes are named by their **solvent**: **oil** varnish (durable, slow-drying), **spirit** varnish (fast-drying, less durable — lacquer and French polish), **turpentine**, and **water** varnish.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacquer dries fast because spirit evaporates fast** — and it is less durable for exactly the same reason. Oil varnish is the choice for exterior and hard-wearing work.

questions.stem: Which method of project planning was invented first?
questions.solution:
**Bar chart.**

The techniques appeared in this order, each fixing a limitation of the one before it:

| Order | Technique | Introduced | Advance made |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Bar chart (Gantt chart)** | **c. 1917, Henry Gantt** | Activities shown as horizontal bars against a time scale |
| 2 | Milestone chart | 1940s | Bars broken at key checkpoints, so progress within a bar is visible |
| 3 | **CPM** | 1957, DuPont | **Network** logic; deterministic durations; identifies the critical path |
| 4 | **PERT** | 1958, US Navy Polaris | Network with **probabilistic** durations (t_{o}, t_{m}, t_{p}) |

The **bar chart** is therefore the earliest, and remains the most widely used for communication because it is immediately readable. Its weakness is decisive for control, though: it shows *when* activities happen but not **why** — the interdependencies are invisible, so it cannot show which delay matters and which does not.

The **milestone chart** was the intermediate improvement, inserting identifiable events within long bars.

The network methods answered the real gap by making **logic explicit**. CPM and PERT differ mainly in their treatment of duration:

| | CPM | PERT |
|---|---|---|
| Duration | **Deterministic**, single estimate | **Probabilistic**, three estimates |
| Expected time | — | t_{e} = (t_{o} + 4t_{m} + t_{p})/6 |
| Orientation | **Activity**-oriented | **Event**-oriented |
| Suits | Repetitive work — construction | Novel work — research, development |

In modern practice the two have largely merged, and planning software presents network logic while still displaying it as a bar chart.

examTip.trick: The chronology: **Gantt (bar) chart, 1910s → CPM and PERT, late 1950s → precedence diagrams and modern software**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar chart came first and is still the best COMMUNICATION tool** — anyone can read it. What it cannot show is **dependency** and hence the **critical path**, which is exactly the gap CPM and PERT were invented to fill. Modern practice uses networks to compute and bar charts to present.

questions.stem: Which engineer is registered in category A by the Nepal Engineering Council?
questions.solution:
**General Engineer.**

The Nepal Engineering Council maintains its register in three categories:

| Category | Registrant |
|---|---|
| **A** | **General Engineer** |
| B | Professional Engineer |
| C | Foreign Engineer |

**Category A — General Engineer** is the ordinary registration granted to an engineer holding a recognised Nepali or equivalent engineering degree, on passing the registration examination. This is the category the license examination in this syllabus leads to, and it is what permits general practice of the profession in Nepal.

**Category B — Professional Engineer** is the higher grade, requiring substantial professional experience beyond the degree in addition to registration.

**Category C — Foreign Engineer** covers a non-Nepali engineer registered to practise in Nepal, normally for a specified project and period.

The framework comes from the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**, under which the Council registers engineers, recognises qualifications, conducts the registration examination and regulates professional conduct.

Two related facts examined alongside this: registration is a **legal prerequisite** to practising engineering in Nepal, and it is the Council — not the Nepal Engineers' Association, which is a voluntary professional body — that holds this statutory authority. The Council's chairman must hold a bachelor's degree in engineering with at least **fifteen years'** professional experience, a point tested directly in the next question of this paper.

examTip.trick: The NEC's category structure is set by qualification and scope of practice, with **Category A** as the general engineer's registration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Registration with the NEC is the licensure element of the profession** — it is what makes engineering a regulated profession in Nepal rather than an unrestricted occupation. Practising or signing drawings without it is an offence under the Act.

questions.stem: What is the requirement for being chairman of the Nepal Engineering Council?
options: Bachelor degree and engineering experience of 10 years
Bachelor degree and engineering experience of 15 years
Master degree and engineering experience of 15 years
Master degree and engineering experience of 10 years
questions.solution:
**Bachelor's degree with at least 15 years' experience.**

Section 3 of the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055** sets out the constitution of the Council. The two senior posts are distinguished only by the length of experience required:

| Post | Qualification | Experience |
|---|---|---|
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's degree in engineering | **At least 15 years** |
| **Vice-chairman** | Bachelor's degree in engineering | **At least 10 years** |

Both are **nominated by the Government** from among practising engineers. Note that a master's degree is **not** required for either post — which is what options (c) and (d) are placed to catch.

The full composition of the Council, worth knowing since it is examined as a list:
- Chairman — nominated engineer, bachelor's degree, 15 years' experience
- Vice-chairman — nominated engineer, bachelor's degree, 10 years' experience
- Five engineers nominated by the Government
- President, Nepal Engineers' Association
- Five engineers **elected** by the Nepal Engineers' Association
- One Campus Chief nominated by the Government from among engineering college campus chiefs
- One representative, Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University
- Two engineers nominated by the Council
- **Registrar — Member-Secretary**

Nominations and elections to the two five-member groups must be made **subject-wise**, drawing from separate branches of engineering, so that the Council is not dominated by one discipline.

examTip.trick: Chairman and vice-chairman are both **nominated by the Government**, and both need a bachelor's degree — the difference is the experience required.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chairman 15 years, vice-chairman 10 years.** Also worth holding: **five engineers nominated by the Government, and TWO nominated by the Council itself** — that last figure is a favourite question.

questions.stem: A disease which is widespread and can reach globally is termed as:
questions.solution:
**Pandemic.**

The four terms are distinguished purely by **geographical extent and persistence**, and the question specifies global reach:

| Term | Meaning | Extent |
|---|---|---|
| **Endemic** | Constantly present at a fairly steady rate in a population | **Confined** to a locality or region |
| **Epidemic** | A sudden outbreak, cases rising well above the expected level | A community, locality or **region** |
| **Pandemic** | An epidemic that has crossed **national borders and continents** | **Global** |
| Hyper-endemic | Persistently present at a **high** level in a population | Local, but intense |

A pandemic is, in short, **an epidemic gone global** — the disease has spread across multiple countries or continents. Since the question asks for the term describing a disease that is "widespread and can reach globally", **pandemic** is the only correct choice.

Examples for orientation: malaria is **endemic** to parts of the Terai; a seasonal cholera outbreak in one district is an **epidemic**; COVID-19 and the 1918 influenza were **pandemics**.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The widely-copied answer sheet keys this as (a), epidemic. That is wrong on its own terms: the explanatory note printed directly beneath it states that "a pandemic is a global epidemic, meaning the disease has spread across multiple countries or continents" — which is a definition of option (c), not option (a). An epidemic is by definition bounded by a community or region, so it cannot be the answer to a question that specifies global reach. The answer is (c).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (a), epidemic. The question specifies a disease that is widespread and reaches globally, which is the definition of a pandemic. The source's own printed explanation states that a pandemic is a global epidemic, contradicting its own key. Answer corrected to (c).

examTip.trick: The ladder by geographic spread: **endemic** (constantly present in an area), **outbreak** (a sudden local rise), **epidemic** (spreading through a community or region), **pandemic** (crossing countries and continents).
examTip.mnemonic: **Pan = all, demos = people.** Endemic is about *persistence*; epidemic and pandemic are about *spread*.

questions.stem: In incremental analysis, which project is selected as the base alternative?
questions.solution:
**The project with the lower initial investment.**

Incremental analysis asks, of each successive step up in investment, whether the **extra** money earns at least the minimum attractive rate of return. For that question to be meaningful the increments must all be positive, so the analysis must start from the cheapest alternative — the **defender** — and work upward.

The procedure:
1. Rank all mutually exclusive alternatives in **increasing order of initial investment**.
2. Take the alternative with the **lowest** investment (or the do-nothing option) as the current defender.
3. Compute the incremental cash flow to the next-larger alternative — the **challenger** — and its incremental rate of return, Δ IRR.
4. If **Δ IRR ≥ MARR**, the challenger becomes the new defender; otherwise it is discarded.
5. Repeat until one alternative survives; that is the choice.

Starting anywhere else would leave a cheaper alternative untested and could recommend spending money that never earns its keep.

**Why incremental analysis is needed at all.** Ranking alternatives by their individual IRR can give the wrong answer, because a small project with a spectacular rate of return may leave most of the available capital idle. Only the incremental test asks the right question: *is this additional expenditure justified?* Note also that maximising **NPV** at the MARR gives the same choice as a correct incremental IRR analysis — the two agree when the increments are evaluated properly, and it is the naive comparison of individual IRRs that misleads.

This is the same principle as Set 1 Q15, which asked for the same fact from the other direction: the initial investment of the base alternative must be the **minimum**.

examTip.trick: Incremental analysis tests whether each **extra** rupee of investment earns its keep, so you must begin from the **cheapest** alternative and step upward one comparison at a time.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rank by increasing investment, then test each increment against the minimum attractive rate of return.** Starting from the most expensive option inverts every subsequent comparison and can select the wrong project entirely.

questions.stem: Which roller is used for compacting clayey soils?
questions.solution:
**Sheep-footed (sheep's foot) roller**, also called a **tamping** or pad-foot roller.

Clay is **cohesive**. Its particles are held together by cohesion and adsorbed water, and vibration does almost nothing to rearrange them. What clay needs is **kneading and manipulation** — a shearing, remoulding action that breaks down the clods and forces out air.

A sheep-foot roller has a steel drum studded with projecting rectangular feet arranged in a staggered pattern. Each foot penetrates the layer and delivers a concentrated static pressure with a kneading action as it enters and withdraws, compacting the layer **from the bottom upwards**. That is exactly the mechanism cohesive soil requires.

Match each roller to its soil, since the question is asked both ways round:

| Roller | Action | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Sheep-foot / tamping** | **Kneading + static pressure** | **Clay, silty clay — cohesive soils** |
| Vibratory | Dynamic vibration | Sand, gravel, rockfill — cohesionless |
| Pneumatic tyred | Kneading, static | Both fine and coarse; also bituminous layers |
| Smooth wheeled (static) | Static weight | Finishing, proof rolling, asphalt surfacing |

The single principle to carry: **cohesive soils need kneading, cohesionless soils need vibration.** Set 1 Q50 asked the mirror-image question — which roller for coarse-grained soil — and the answer there was the vibratory roller.

Note too that clay must be compacted at close to its **optimum moisture content** (from the Proctor test, IS 2720 Part 7) in thin layers of 150 to 300 mm; too dry and the clods will not break down, too wet and the pore water cannot escape.

examTip.trick: Match the roller to the soil's mechanism: a **sheepsfoot** roller's feet **knead and remould** cohesive soil, breaking down clods and compacting from the bottom up as it walks out. Vibration does that job for **granular** soil.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kneading for clay, vibration for sand.** Vibrating a clay achieves little because the water cannot escape quickly — the same compaction-versus-consolidation distinction that runs through soil mechanics.

questions.stem: One of the probable causes of rutting on flexible pavements is:
options: Excessive stripping of binder material from the wearing course
Use of flaky aggregates in the wearing course
questions.solution:
**Inadequate compaction of pavement layers.**

**Rutting** is a longitudinal depression that forms in the wheel paths of a flexible pavement — a **permanent deformation** accumulated under repeated traffic loading.

If a layer has not been compacted to its specified density, it retains excess air voids and its particles are not interlocked. Under each passing axle the material densifies a little further and shears laterally, and those small permanent strains accumulate into a visible rut. Because the deficiency can lie in the **base or sub-base** as well as the surfacing, inadequate compaction is the most fundamental and common cause.

The other options are real distresses but not the primary cause of rutting:
- **Stripping** of binder from the aggregate is caused by water and leads to **ravelling and potholes** — loss of material, not deformation.
- **Flaky aggregates** crush and degrade under load, contributing to deformation, but this is a secondary factor; the flakiness index is limited to about 25% for this reason.
- **High wind speeds** have no bearing on pavement deformation at all.

The other contributors worth listing: excess bitumen or too soft a grade, insufficient stability in the mix (low Marshall stability), overloaded axles, high pavement temperature, and a weak or wet subgrade.

Distinguish rutting from the neighbouring distresses that get confused with it:

| Distress | Appearance | Main cause |
|---|---|---|
| **Rutting** | **Longitudinal depression in wheel path** | **Inadequate compaction; permanent deformation** |
| Corrugation | Regular transverse ripples | Excess or soft binder, unstable mix |
| Shoving | Localised bulging, at junctions and stops | Braking and acceleration on an unstable mix |
| Ravelling | Progressive loss of aggregate | Stripping, insufficient binder |
| Alligator cracking | Interconnected fatigue cracks | Repeated loading, weak subgrade |

examTip.trick: **Rutting** is a permanent longitudinal depression in the wheel paths — an **accumulated deformation** failure, not a cracking failure. So its causes are inadequate compaction, excess bitumen, a weak mix, or an under-strength subgrade.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rutting = deformation (too soft or under-compacted). Cracking = fatigue or ageing (too brittle).** The two failure families need opposite remedies, so diagnosing which one you have is the first step in any pavement investigation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is used for speed regulation?
questions.solution:
**85th percentile speed.**

A spot-speed study produces a cumulative frequency curve of observed speeds, and different percentiles from that one curve serve different purposes. The **85th percentile** — the speed at or below which 85% of vehicles travel — is the accepted basis for setting the **safe speed limit**.

The reasoning is behavioural rather than theoretical. Most drivers choose a speed that is reasonable for the conditions, so the bulk of the distribution represents sensible behaviour. Setting the limit at the 85th percentile accommodates that majority and targets only the fastest 15%, the genuine outliers. A limit set much lower is widely disobeyed, loses legitimacy, and *increases* the speed variance — and it is speed **variance**, more than absolute speed, that correlates with crashes.

The percentiles and their uses:

| Percentile | Used for |
|---|---|
| **98th** | **Geometric design speed** — sight distances, curve radii, superelevation |
| **85th** | **Safe speed limit / speed regulation** |
| 50th (median) | Average speed of the traffic stream |
| **15th** | **Minimum speed limit** — slow vehicles obstruct and cause overtaking conflicts |

So the design engineer uses the **98th** percentile (design for the fast driver, so the geometry is safe for nearly everyone) while the regulator uses the **85th**. Confusing the two is the trap this question sets, and option (a) is there for exactly that.

Related speed definitions: **spot speed** (at a point, measured by enoscope or radar), **running speed** (distance ÷ time in motion) and **journey speed** (distance ÷ total time including stops). The difference between running and journey speed measures the delay in the system.

examTip.trick: Speed limits are set at the **85th percentile** speed — the speed below which 85% of drivers travel. It is used because most drivers choose a reasonable speed, and a limit far below it is ignored and unenforceable.
examTip.mnemonic: **85th percentile sets the speed LIMIT; 15th percentile the MINIMUM; 98th percentile is used for GEOMETRIC DESIGN**, because the road must be safe even for the fastest drivers. Three percentiles, three different purposes.

questions.stem: Bulking of coarse aggregate is:
questions.solution:
**Negligible.**

Bulking is caused by **surface tension** in the thin water film around each damp particle: the films hold neighbouring grains apart, so the same mass occupies a larger volume.

The effect depends on **surface area per unit volume**. Fine aggregate has an enormous specific surface, so a large number of tiny films separate a large number of small grains and the bulk volume grows appreciably — **20 to 40%** for sand, peaking at about 4 to 6% moisture content, and finer sand bulks more.

Coarse aggregate has a very small specific surface by comparison. The few water films are negligible relative to the size of the particles they surround, and they cannot hold 20 mm stones apart in any meaningful way. So bulking of coarse aggregate is **negligible** and is ignored in practice.

| | Fine aggregate (sand) | Coarse aggregate |
|---|---|---|
| Specific surface | Very high | Low |
| **Bulking** | **20–40%** | **Negligible** |
| Correction needed in volume batching? | **Yes** | No |

**The practical consequence.** When batching **by volume**, the sand quantity must be increased to correct for bulking, or the mix will be sand-deficient — harsh, difficult to finish and lower in strength. No such correction is applied to the coarse aggregate. Batching **by weight** avoids the problem entirely, which is one of the main arguments for weigh-batching.

Note also that bulking vanishes at **full saturation**: inundated sand occupies the same volume as dry sand, which is the basis of the field test by inundation (IS 2386 Part 3). Set 1 Q55 asked the companion question about what bulking of sand actually means.

examTip.trick: Bulking is caused by **moisture films holding grains apart**, and the effect depends on the **surface area to volume ratio**. Coarse aggregate has very little surface area per unit volume, so the effect is negligible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine sand bulks 20–30%; coarse aggregate essentially not at all.** Which is why the correction matters for sand batching and not for stone.

questions.stem: For a two hinged arch having constant EI, the horizontal thrust H at a point (x, y) on the arch, in terms of the beam moment M, is given by:
questions.solution:
**∫ M·y·(dy/dx) ÷ ∫ y²·(ds/EI)** — that is, **H = ∫(My ds/EI) / ∫(y² ds/EI)**.

A two-hinged arch is **indeterminate to the first degree**: there are four unknown reactions (two components at each hinge) against three equations of equilibrium. The vertical reactions come from taking moments about either support; the redundant is the **horizontal thrust H**.

**The compatibility condition.** Both supports are hinged and immovable, so the horizontal displacement of one relative to the other must be zero. By Castigliano's second theorem that means

> ∂U/∂H = 0

Carrying that through with the strain energy of bending, where the net moment at any section is (M − Hy) with M the simple-beam moment at the same section, gives

> **H = ∫(M·y·ds/EI) / ∫(y²·ds/EI)**

For constant EI the flexural rigidity cancels from numerator and denominator, so
> H = ∫My ds / ∫y² ds

**How to pick the option without recalling the derivation.** The denominator must carry **y²**, because it arises from differentiating (M − Hy)² with respect to H. That single observation eliminates (a), which has y³, and (b), which has y. Between (c) and (d), the numerator must be **linear in M** — the compatibility equation is linear in the applied loading — so the M y² of option (c) is wrong. Only **(d)** survives.

The contrast with a **three-hinged** arch is worth holding: that structure is **determinate**, and its thrust follows from simple statics by taking moments about the crown hinge, H = M_{c}/y_{c} — no integration and no EI needed. That is what makes Q62 of this same paper a much shorter calculation than this one.

examTip.trick: The horizontal thrust of a two-hinged arch is found by **strain energy**: release the horizontal restraint, and require that the horizontal deflection be zero. Castigliano's ∂U/∂H = 0 gives the ratio of the two integrals.
examTip.mnemonic: **A two-hinged arch is indeterminate to degree 1; a three-hinged arch is DETERMINATE** — the third hinge supplies the extra equation. That is why three-hinged arches are used where **settlement or temperature movement** is expected: being determinate, they develop no self-stress.

questions.stem: Kaplan turbine is:
questions.solution:
**A low head, axial flow turbine** — and a reaction turbine.

The Kaplan runner looks like a ship's propeller: water enters through a spiral casing and guide vanes, is turned to flow **parallel to the axis of rotation** through the runner, and leaves through a draft tube. Only three to six blades are used, so the flow passage is very open — which is what lets it pass a large discharge.

Its characteristics all follow from that geometry:

| Property | Kaplan |
|---|---|
| Type | **Reaction** (pressure drops across the runner) |
| Flow direction | **Axial** |
| Head | **Low — below about 30 m** |
| Discharge | **Very high** |
| Specific speed | High, 300–1000 |
| Draft tube | Required |
| Blades | **Adjustable** (pitch varies with load) |

The adjustable blades are the Kaplan's distinguishing advantage: because both the guide vanes and the runner blades move, it holds high efficiency across a wide range of part load, where a fixed-blade propeller turbine falls away sharply.

Compare across the family, since the options mix the categories deliberately:

| Turbine | Type | Flow | Head |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pelton | **Impulse** | Tangential | Very high, > 250 m |
| Francis | Reaction | **Mixed** (radial in, axial out) | Medium, 25–250 m |
| **Kaplan** | Reaction | **Axial** | **Low, < 30 m** |

So option (a) wrongly calls it an impulse turbine, (b) wrongly calls it outward-flow radial, and (d) describes a **Francis** turbine at high head. Nepal's high-head run-of-river schemes favour Pelton and Francis units; Kaplan turbines suit low-head sites on large rivers in the Terai.

examTip.trick: Match turbine to head: **Pelton high head/low flow (impulse), Francis medium head (mixed flow reaction), Kaplan low head/high flow (axial flow reaction)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kaplan's blades are ADJUSTABLE**, which is what lets it hold high efficiency across a wide flow range — essential on a low-head river where the discharge varies seasonally. A fixed-blade version of the same machine is a **propeller** turbine.

questions.stem: The function of a surge tank is to:
options: Relieve water hammer pressures in the penstock pipe
questions.solution:
**Relieve water hammer pressures in the penstock pipe.**

When the turbine gates close suddenly, the momentum of the water column in a long conduit cannot vanish instantly, and a pressure wave — **water hammer** — travels back up the pipe. Unrelieved, the pressure rise can burst the penstock or damage the runner and spiral casing.

A surge tank is an open-topped shaft placed at the junction of the low-pressure tunnel and the high-pressure penstock. It works in both directions:

- **On sudden closure**, it accepts the rejected water, so the level in the shaft rises and the pressure surge is converted into a harmless change of water level. The water-hammer pressure is then confined to the short length of penstock **below** the tank instead of travelling the whole tunnel.
- **On sudden opening**, it supplies water immediately from its own storage while the flow in the long tunnel accelerates, preventing negative pressure and cavitation.

Option (c) inverts the purpose — the tank **absorbs** surge, it does not produce it. Option (a) describes a different device: constant pressure at delivery is the job of a **pressure reducing valve** or a balancing reservoir, not a surge tank.

Types: simple, restricted orifice, **differential (Johnson)**, and inclined. The restricted orifice and differential types damp the oscillation faster by throttling the flow into the shaft.

A surge tank is provided when the penstock is long relative to the head — where it is impractical, a **pressure relief valve** is used instead. Set 1 Q45 asked the same fact from the other direction, naming the surge tank as the device that protects the turbine and runner from damage.

examTip.trick: The surge tank gives the decelerating water column a **free surface** to rise into, converting a destructive pressure wave into a slow rise and fall of level.
examTip.mnemonic: **It protects only what is UPSTREAM of it** — the long tunnel. The short penstock below still takes the full water hammer and is designed for it. It also **supplies water instantly on load acceptance**, before the long tunnel column can accelerate.

questions.stem: On the basis of hydraulic design, a dam is classified as:
questions.solution:
**Overflow and non-overflow dam.**

Dams are classified on three different bases, and the question specifies the **hydraulic** one — how the structure handles water passing over it:

| Basis | Classification |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic design** | **Overflow (spillway section) and non-overflow** |
| **Function / use** | **Storage, diversion, detention, debris** dam |
| **Material and structural action** | Gravity, **arch**, **buttress**, embankment (earthfill / rockfill), timber, steel |

An **overflow dam** — the spillway section — is designed for water to pass over its crest, so its downstream profile is shaped (usually as an ogee) to keep the nappe attached, and it needs an **energy dissipation** arrangement at the toe: a stilling basin, roller bucket or ski jump.

A **non-overflow dam** is designed so that water never passes over it. Its crest is set above the maximum water level plus freeboard, and it may be built of material such as earthfill that overtopping would destroy — which is precisely why an embankment dam must always have a separate spillway in a competent section.

Why the others are wrong: **storage, diversion and detention** classify by *purpose*, so options (a) and (b) belong to the functional classification; **arch and buttress** classify by *structural action*, which is option (d).

A large scheme normally combines both hydraulic types in one barrier — a concrete overflow spillway section flanked by non-overflow embankment sections, as at Bhakra or Kulekhani.

examTip.trick: Dams are classified several ways and the question specifies **hydraulic design** — meaning whether water passes **over** the dam or not.
examTip.mnemonic: **By hydraulic design: overflow (spillway section) and non-overflow. By material: earth, rockfill, concrete, masonry. By structural action: gravity, arch, buttress, embankment.** Read which classification is being asked for.

questions.stem: The structure provided to discharge extra water from a canal is:
questions.solution:
**Canal escape.**

A canal escape is a **safety valve**. It is a side channel taken off the canal and led to a natural drain, river or depression, so that surplus water can be let out whenever the canal carries more than it should. Without one, an unexpected inflow — a sudden rainstorm on the command, or a rapid closure of outlets downstream — would overtop the banks and breach them.

When an escape is used:
- Rejected supply when demand falls suddenly downstream.
- Surplus from rainfall entering the canal.
- **Emptying the canal** for inspection, repair or closure at the end of a season.

The main canal appurtenances, each with a distinct job, which is exactly what this question tests:

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Canal escape** | **Discharge surplus water out of the canal** |
| Canal regulator | **Control the discharge** entering a canal or distributary |
| Canal fall (drop) | Lower the bed level where the ground slopes more steeply than the canal, dissipating surplus energy |
| Canal outlet (module) | Deliver the sanctioned share of water to a **watercourse / field** |
| Cross-drainage work | Carry the canal past a natural drainage — aqueduct, syphon, super-passage |

So a **regulator** controls what comes in, an **outlet** delivers to the farmer, a **fall** deals with ground slope, and only the **escape** disposes of excess.

Types of escape: **surplus water escape** (weir type, operating automatically once the level rises above the crest) and **tail escape** at the end of a canal, which also helps maintain the tail-end supply.

examTip.trick: Distinguish the canal structures by purpose: an **escape** discharges **surplus water out** of the canal; a **regulator** controls flow into or along it; an **outlet** delivers to a watercourse; a **fall** takes the bed down a step.
examTip.mnemonic: **Escape = emergency exit for the water.** It protects the canal banks from overtopping when the demand suddenly falls (a closed outlet downstream) or after unexpected rainfall inflow.

questions.stem: The structure at the head of a regulator to remove silt is:
questions.solution:
**Silt excluder.**

The distinction turns entirely on **where** the device sits and therefore **whether the silt ever enters the canal**:

| Device | Location | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Silt excluder** | **At the head regulator, in the river** | **Prevents** silt from entering the canal at all |
| Silt ejector (extractor) | **In the canal**, some distance downstream of the head | **Removes** silt that has already entered |

A **silt excluder** is a set of horizontal tunnels built into the floor of the river pocket immediately upstream of the head regulator. Because the sediment concentration in a river is greatest near the bed, the tunnels skim off the **bottom, silt-laden layer** and pass it downstream through the barrage undersluices, while the **clearer upper layer** flows over the tunnel roofs and into the canal. It excludes silt at source — which is why the question's phrase "at the head of regulator" points to it.

A **silt ejector**, by contrast, is placed in the canal itself. Silt that has already entered settles into a tunnel below the canal bed and is ejected back to the river or a drain. **Silt extractor** is simply another name for the ejector, which is why options (a) and (c) describe the same device and neither can be the answer.

Prevention being cheaper than cure, an excluder is preferred where the site allows; ejectors are provided as a second line of defence on canals drawing from heavily silt-laden rivers — a real concern for Nepal's Terai canals fed by Himalayan rivers with very high sediment loads.

The underlying principle is the same one exploited by a **settling basin** in a hydropower intake: sediment concentrates near the bed, so the flow can be split into a clean upper layer and a dirty lower one.

examTip.trap: **Silt EXCLUDER** and **silt EJECTOR** are different structures and are constantly swapped.
examTip.trick: An **excluder** sits at the **head regulator** and stops silt **entering** the canal in the first place, by drawing the clear upper water in and passing the silt-laden bottom water on downstream. An **ejector** sits **inside the canal** and removes silt that has **already entered**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Excluder EXCLUDES at the entrance; ejector EJECTS from within.** Prevention versus cure.

questions.stem: Launching apron is made of:
questions.solution:
**Gabion** — stone-filled wire crates, or loose stone pitching of similar character.

A launching apron is laid horizontally on the river bed at the toe of a guide bank or spur. Its job is not to resist water directly but to **follow the bed down as it scours**. When the river deepens the scour hole, the stone at the edge of the apron slides — "launches" — down the face of the hole and armours it, protecting the toe of the structure from being undermined.

That function dictates the material. The apron must be **flexible and self-adjusting**, able to deform and re-lay itself as the bed changes shape. **Gabions** are ideal: the wire mesh holds the stone together as a mattress that can flex and settle without disintegrating, while individual stones can still redistribute.

Why the rigid options fail:
- **Stone masonry and brick masonry** are bonded with mortar into a rigid slab. As soon as the bed scours beneath it, the slab cracks, breaks up and is washed away — it cannot launch.
- **Concrete** in a monolithic slab has the same problem; concrete *blocks*, laid loose, can serve as an apron, but a rigid concrete apron cannot.

Design points examined alongside: the apron is laid to a thickness of about **1.25 t** where t is the thickness of the launched layer, extends about **1.5 D** from the structure (D being the anticipated scour depth below the bed), and launches at a slope of about **2H : 1V**. Scour depth is estimated from **Lacey's regime depth**, R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}, with the design scour taken as a multiple of R depending on the location — deepest at the nose of a guide bank.

This pairs with Q76 of this same paper, which asks for the lengths of the guide banks such an apron protects.

examTip.trick: A launching apron is a reserve of stone laid on the bed that **falls (launches) into the scour hole** as the bed erodes, armouring the slope and stopping the scour progressing toward the structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is designed to be UNDERMINED — that is how it works.** Gabions (wire crates of local boulders) suit Nepali rivers because they are flexible, use local material, and stay together as they launch. Loose stone can be washed away instead.

questions.stem: Saline soil can be improved by:
questions.solution:
**Leaching.**

A **saline** soil has a high concentration of **soluble salts** but a low exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP below 15) and a pH of about 7.5 to 8.5. The salts are simply *present* in the soil water; they have not displaced calcium and magnesium from the clay exchange complex.

Because the problem is soluble salt, the remedy is **physical removal** — apply good-quality water (itself low in salt, under about 1500 to 2000 ppm) in excess of the crop requirement, dissolve the salts, and flush them **below the root zone**. That is leaching. It requires adequate **drainage**: without a way for the water to escape, leaching merely raises the water table and the salts return by capillary rise on evaporation.

The crucial contrast is with the **sodic (alkali)** soil, and this pair is examined constantly:

| | **Saline soil** | **Sodic / alkali soil** |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | High **soluble salts** | High **exchangeable sodium** |
| ESP | < 15 | **> 15** |
| pH | 7.5 – 8.5 | **> 8.5** |
| Structure | Retained, flocculated | **Destroyed** — clay deperses, soil becomes impermeable |
| **Remedy** | **Leaching with drainage** | **Gypsum (CaSO₄) or pyrite**, then leaching |

So **gypsum** — option (c) — is the answer to a question about a **sodic** soil, not a saline one: the calcium replaces sodium on the exchange sites, the clay reflocculates, permeability is restored, and only then can the displaced sodium sulphate be leached out. **Pyrite** works similarly by generating acid. **Lime** is used to correct **acid** soils and would make an already alkaline soil worse.

Remember the sequence for sodic soil: **amend first, leach second** — leaching alone cannot help while the soil remains impermeable.

examTip.trick: **Leaching** floods the soil with good-quality water so that the soluble salts **dissolve and drain away below the root zone**. It only works if there is somewhere for the water to go.
examTip.mnemonic: **Leaching REQUIRES adequate DRAINAGE** — without it, the water table simply rises and the salts return by capillary action. That is why **waterlogging and salinity are treated together**, and why drainage is the foundation of both remedies.

questions.stem: What is the main objective of toxicity assessment?
options: To determine the source of pathway
To estimate how much of a substance does what kind of harm
questions.solution:
**To estimate how much of a substance causes what kind of harm** — the dose–response relationship.

Toxicity assessment establishes the link between the **quantity** of a substance received and the **nature and severity** of the health effect it produces. It answers the question "how much is harmful, and harmful in what way?" — not merely how much is present.

The distinction the options are testing is that the other three are **separate steps** of a risk assessment, each answering a different question:

| Step | Question answered |
|---|---|
| Hazard identification | Can this substance cause harm at all? |
| **Dose–response (toxicity) assessment** | **How much causes how much harm?** |
| **Exposure assessment** | Who is exposed, by what pathway, to what dose? |
| Risk characterisation | Combining the above — what is the actual risk? |

So option (a) belongs to **pathway analysis**, option (d) to **exposure assessment**, and option (b) is merely **measurement of concentration** — a monitoring result, which tells you nothing about harm until it is set against a dose–response curve.

The quantities toxicity assessment produces are the ones used in standard setting:
- **LD₅₀ / LC₅₀** — the dose or concentration lethal to 50% of a test population; a measure of acute toxicity.
- **NOAEL** — no observed adverse effect level.
- **ADI or RfD** — acceptable daily intake or reference dose, derived from the NOAEL by applying safety factors.

For carcinogens the assumption is usually that **no threshold exists**, so risk is expressed as a probability per unit dose rather than as a safe level. This is the basis on which drinking-water limits such as 0.01 mg/L for arsenic are set.

examTip.trick: Toxicology is fundamentally about **dose and response** — establishing what quantity of a substance produces what degree of harm.
examTip.mnemonic: **"The dose makes the poison."** Everything is toxic at some dose; nothing is toxic at none. That principle is what underlies every drinking-water standard, exposure limit and permissible discharge concentration.

questions.stem: Use of chlorine in water does not reduce:
questions.solution:
**Dissolved oxygen.**

Chlorine is an **oxidising agent**. It supplies the oxidising power itself rather than consuming oxygen already dissolved in the water, so chlorination does **not** deplete dissolved oxygen. That is the key distinction: chlorine demand and oxygen demand are different things.

What chlorine *does* react with, and therefore reduces:

| Constituent | Reaction |
|---|---|
| **Ammonia** | Forms **chloramines** — mono-, di- and tri-chloramine. This is combined residual chlorine, a weaker but longer-lasting disinfectant |
| **Organic matter** | Oxidised; also forms **trihalomethanes (THMs)**, a disinfection by-product of health concern |
| **Iron and manganese** | Oxidised from soluble Fe²⁺/Mn²⁺ to insoluble Fe³⁺/Mn⁴⁺, which then precipitate and are filtered out |
| Hydrogen sulphide, taste and odour compounds | Oxidised |
| Pathogens | Inactivated — the primary purpose |

All of these constitute the **chlorine demand**: the dose consumed before any free residual appears.

The idea that organises this is **breakpoint chlorination**. As the dose rises, chlorine first satisfies the reducing agents (iron, manganese, sulphide), then combines with ammonia to form chloramines, whose concentration peaks and then **falls** as further chlorine oxidises them to nitrogen. Past that minimum — the **breakpoint** — additional chlorine survives as **free residual chlorine**, which is the effective disinfectant.

Nepal's drinking-water standard requires a **free residual chlorine of 0.1 to 0.2 mg/L** at the consumer's tap, with a minimum contact time of **30 minutes**. Efficiency falls as pH rises, since the potent HOCl gives way to the much weaker OCl⁻ — the point tested in Q75 of this same paper.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Chlorine reduces bacteria, taste, odour and some colour — it does **not** reduce dissolved oxygen.
examTip.trick: Chlorine is an **oxidising disinfectant**. It kills pathogens and oxidises taste- and odour-causing compounds, but DO is a physical property of the water, not something chlorine consumes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorine's job is disinfection.** Watch for the by-products: reacting with natural organic matter it forms **trihalomethanes**, which are themselves regulated — hence the balance between adequate residual and minimising THMs.

questions.stem: Vertical formwork of a column can be removed after:
questions.solution:
**24 hours** (IS 456 gives 16 to 24 hours).

Vertical formwork to a column, wall or beam side carries **no load from the concrete except lateral pressure while it is still fluid**. Once the concrete has set and can stand under its own weight, the side shuttering has nothing left to do, so it may be struck very early — within 16 to 24 hours.

Contrast this with **soffit** formwork, which supports the **self-weight of the concrete in bending**. That cannot be removed until the member has developed enough flexural strength, which takes days.

The full table from IS 456 cl. 11.3, which is worth memorising in full because any row can be asked:

| Formwork | Minimum period before striking |
|---|---|
| **Vertical formwork to columns, walls, beam sides** | **16 – 24 hours** |
| Soffit formwork to slabs (props re-fixed at once) | **3 days** |
| Soffit formwork to beams (props re-fixed at once) | **7 days** |
| Props to slabs — span up to 4.5 m | 7 days |
| Props to slabs — span over 4.5 m | **14 days** |
| Props to beams and arches — span up to 6 m | 14 days |
| Props to beams and arches — span over 6 m | **21 days** |

Two patterns make the table easier to hold: the period lengthens as the **span** increases, and **props** always stay far longer than the sheeting they support — which is why the code allows the soffit sheeting to come off a slab at 3 days provided the props are immediately re-fixed.

These periods assume ordinary Portland cement and normal temperature; they must be extended for cold weather, for cement replacement materials, and for members carrying construction loads. Striking early is a common cause of sagging and cracking in slabs.
