examTip.trick: Vertical faces carry **no load** once the concrete has set — only the props under **soffits** hold weight. That is the whole reason for the difference.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sides 16–24 hours; soffits 7 days for slabs, up to 21 days for beam props spanning over 6 m.** Confusing the two figures is the trap, and striking soffit props early is a real cause of collapse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an obstacle to chaining but not to ranging?
questions.solution:
**River.**

The two operations are obstructed by different things, and the classification follows from what each one needs:

- **Chaining** requires physically laying a chain or tape along the ground — so anything you cannot walk across stops it.
- **Ranging** requires only an **unobstructed line of sight** between stations.

A **river** blocks chaining, because the tape cannot be laid across the water, but the banks are visible to one another, so ranging is unaffected. That makes it the classic **obstacle to chaining but not to ranging**, and the distance across is found by geometry — setting out a right-angled or similar-triangle construction on the bank and computing the gap.

The standard classification:

| Obstacle | Chaining | Ranging | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Obstruction to **chaining only** | Blocked | **Free** | **River, pond, lake** |
| Obstruction to **ranging only** | Free | Blocked | Intervening **hillock** or rising ground |
| Obstruction to **both** | Blocked | Blocked | **Building**, dense wood |

So a **hillock** (option b) is the mirror-image case: you can chain over it by stepping, but you cannot see across it, so it obstructs ranging and is solved by **reciprocal ranging**. A **building** (option a) obstructs both, and is dealt with by setting out perpendicular offsets around it.

The general method for all such cases is the same: replace the blocked measurement with a **computable geometric construction** — congruent or similar triangles, or a right-angle offset — and reduce the obstacle to a calculation.

examTip.trick: Sort obstacles by what they block: a **river** can be **seen** across (so ranging is possible) but cannot be **measured** across directly (so chaining is obstructed). A hill blocks vision but not chaining; a building blocks both.
examTip.mnemonic: **River: chaining only. Hill: ranging only. Building: both.** Each case has its own geometric solution — for a river, a triangle set out on the bank.

questions.stem: The reserve of water for the breakdown period is generally not more than …… of total storage.
questions.solution:
**25%.**

A service reservoir's capacity is made up of three distinct components, each meeting a different contingency:

| Component | Purpose | Share of total |
|---|---|---|
| **Balancing (equalising) storage** | Evens out the mismatch between steady pumping and fluctuating hourly demand | Largest — typically about a third to half of the maximum daily demand |
| **Breakdown storage** | Maintains supply while a pump, main or treatment unit is out of service | **Not more than about 25%** |
| **Fire storage** | Meets the short, heavy draw of fire fighting | Sized from a fire-demand formula |

The **breakdown reserve** — sometimes called emergency storage — is what keeps water flowing during a pump failure, a power outage or a main repair. It is commonly taken as **1.5 to 2 hours of the maximum daily demand**, which works out at roughly a quarter of the total reservoir capacity.

Why it is capped rather than made generous: storage is expensive, it occupies elevated land, and water held too long **loses its chlorine residual and deteriorates in quality**. Beyond about 25% the extra security is not worth the cost or the stagnation risk — better to provide **standby pumping units and duplicate mains** so that breakdowns are shorter in the first place.

Related design figures worth carrying: total storage is usually provided for **one third of the maximum daily demand**, service reservoirs are sited to give a residual pressure of about **7 to 17 m** of water at the consumer, and the fire reserve is computed by a formula such as **Kuchling's, Q = 3182√P** — the subject of Set 1 Q70.

examTip.trick: Service reservoir storage is made up of **balancing (equalising) storage, breakdown (emergency) reserve, and fire reserve**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Balancing about 1/3 to 1/2 of daily demand; breakdown up to 25%; fire reserve as computed.** The breakdown reserve exists to keep supply running while a pump or main is repaired — so its size depends on how long a realistic repair takes.

questions.stem: Water to be used in concrete is similar to:
questions.solution:
**Potable water.**

IS 456 takes drinking-quality water as the practical standard for concrete: if water is fit to drink it is generally fit to mix and cure concrete. It is free of the organic matter, silt, oil, acid, alkali and salt that would interfere with hydration or attack the reinforcement, and it is available everywhere without treatment.

**Distilled water** is unnecessary — chemically purer than needed, and absurdly expensive at concrete volumes. Note that purity beyond potable brings no strength benefit, so option (a) is wrong on economic rather than technical grounds.

**Sea water** must be avoided in reinforced concrete. It carries roughly **3.5% dissolved salts**, mostly sodium chloride, and chloride ions destroy the passive film on the steel and initiate **corrosion of the reinforcement**. It also causes efflorescence and a modest loss of long-term strength. It may be tolerated in **unreinforced** mass concrete where no steel is at risk and appearance does not matter.

The limits IS 456 places on mixing and curing water:

| Property | Limit |
|---|---|
| pH | **Not less than 6** |
| Chlorides (Cl⁻) | 500 mg/L for RCC; 2000 mg/L for plain concrete |
| Sulphates (SO₃) | 400 mg/L |
| Organic solids | 200 mg/L |
| Inorganic solids | 3000 mg/L |
| Suspended matter | 2000 mg/L |

The practical acceptance test: the **28-day compressive strength** of cubes made with the water in question must be at least **90%** of that of cubes made with distilled water, and the initial setting time must not differ by more than 30 minutes.

examTip.trick: The working rule is simple and practical: **water fit to drink is fit for concrete**. What matters is the absence of oils, acids, alkalis, salts, sugar and organic matter, all of which interfere with hydration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Potable is the benchmark — but SEA WATER is not acceptable for reinforced concrete**, despite being drinkable to no one and harmless to plain concrete. Its chlorides corrode the reinforcement, which is the real objection.

questions.stem: In a roof truss, the value of snow load is taken as:
questions.solution:
**2.5 N/m² per millimetre depth of snow** — equivalently 2.5 N/m² for each 1 mm of snow depth.

Snow load is computed from the depth of accumulated snow and its unit weight:

> Snow load = 2.5 N/m² × depth of snow in mm

So 100 mm of snow gives 250 N/m², or 0.25 kN/m².

**An important exemption:** if the roof slope exceeds about **50°**, snow load need not be considered at all — the snow slides off rather than accumulating. Conversely, flat and low-pitched roofs, and valleys or parapets where snow **drifts** and piles deeper than the nominal fall, attract the heaviest loads.

The three loads on a roof truss, which are examined as a set:

| Load | Value |
|---|---|
| **Dead load** | Self-weight of truss, purlins and covering. For spacing 4 m and pitch 1:4, self-weight ≈ (L/3 + 6) kg/m² of plan area |
| **Live load** | **0.75 kN/m²** for slope ≤ 10°, with no access. Above 10°, reduce by 0.02 kN/m² for each degree of extra slope |
| **Snow load** | **2.5 N/m² per mm depth**; ignored for slope > 50° |
| Wind load | From IS 875 Part 3 — basic wind speed, terrain and topography factors; usually **suction** on the windward slope of a steep roof |

A point that catches candidates: snow load and live load are **not** added together at full value, because they do not realistically coexist at their maxima — the code takes the more severe of the two.

Wind load is often the governing case for a light truss, and because it acts as suction it can **reverse** the forces in the members, putting into tension what was designed for compression. That reversal must be checked separately.

examTip.trick: Snow load depends on the **depth of snow and its density**, and the code gives the intensity per unit depth. It also depends strongly on **roof slope** — a steep roof sheds snow and takes less.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steeper roof, less snow load** (above about 60° it is usually taken as zero). Snow load matters greatly in Nepal's high-altitude construction, where it can exceed the live load. Watch also for **drifting**, which concentrates snow behind parapets and against walls.

questions.stem: Shear reinforcement is provided in an RC section to:
questions.solution:
**Counteract cracking and shear failure.**

Shear in a beam generates **diagonal tension**. Concrete is weak in tension, so once the principal tensile stress exceeds its capacity, **diagonal cracks** open near the supports, inclined at roughly 45° to the axis. Shear reinforcement — vertical stirrups, inclined stirrups or bent-up bars — crosses those potential crack planes and carries the tension across them, holding the crack closed and allowing the section to carry further load.

Why the alternatives are wrong: bending moment, whether the sagging maximum at mid-span (option a) or the hogging moment at a support (option b), is resisted by **longitudinal** reinforcement — bottom steel for sagging, top steel for hogging. That is a different function and a different set of bars.

**Why it matters so much:** shear failure is **sudden and brittle**, giving no warning, whereas a properly under-reinforced flexural failure is ductile and announces itself through cracking and deflection. Design therefore deliberately makes shear capacity exceed flexural capacity, so that if a beam is overloaded it fails in the gentler mode.

The IS 456 design procedure:
1. Compute the nominal shear stress τ_{v} = V_{u}/(bd).
2. Read the shear strength of the concrete τ_{c} from Table 19, which depends on the grade and on the tension steel percentage.
3. Check τ_{v} against **τ_{c,max}** (Table 20). Exceeding it means the section is too small — no amount of stirrups will do, and the depth must be increased.
4. If τ_{c} < τ_{v} ≤ τ_{c,max}, design stirrups for the excess shear V_{us} = V_{u} − τ_{c}bd, using A_{sv} = V_{us}s_{v}/(0.87f_{y}d).
5. Provide **minimum shear reinforcement** everywhere, even where not required by calculation: A_{sv}/(b·s_{v}) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_{y}).

Maximum stirrup spacing is the least of **0.75d**, 300 mm, or the value from the calculation — close enough that any potential diagonal crack must be crossed by at least one stirrup.

examTip.trick: Shear produces a **principal TENSION at 45°**, and concrete is weak in tension — so it cracks diagonally. Stirrups cross that crack and carry the tension.
examTip.mnemonic: **Diagonal tension is what stirrups resist.** Two further points: shear failure is **sudden and brittle** (unlike ductile flexural failure), which is why **minimum stirrups are required even when not needed by calculation**; and if **τ_v exceeds τ_c,max the SECTION is inadequate** — more stirrups will not help, because the web strut crushes.

questions.stem: Mat is a type of:
questions.solution:
**Shallow foundation.**

A mat — or **raft** — foundation is a single large slab covering the whole or most of the plan area of a structure, carrying all the columns and walls together. Despite its size it is a **shallow** foundation: its depth of embedment is small compared with its width, so D/B is much less than 1 and the load is delivered to the soil immediately beneath it rather than to a deeper stratum.

Do not let the word "large" suggest "deep" — the classification depends on the **depth-to-width ratio**, not on the size of the footing.

| Shallow foundations | Deep foundations |
|---|---|
| Isolated (spread) footing | Pile |
| Combined footing | Pier / drilled shaft |
| Strip / wall footing | Caisson / well foundation |
| **Raft (mat)** | Pile-raft |

**When a raft is chosen:**
- The soil is weak or compressible, so the required area approaches the plan area of the building anyway — the usual rule is that a raft becomes economical once isolated footings would cover more than about **50%** of the plan area.
- **Differential settlement** must be minimised: the raft's stiffness spreads load and makes the structure settle more nearly uniformly.
- There are pockets of soft material or erratic soil, which a raft bridges over.
- A basement is required, or the building must resist **uplift or buoyancy** below the water table — a raft acts as a continuous, watertight slab.

A useful feature is that a raft with a basement can be designed as a **floating or compensated foundation**: the weight of soil excavated offsets the weight of the building, so the net increase in pressure on the ground is small or even zero, and settlement is correspondingly reduced.

Types: flat plate, plate thickened under columns, beam-and-slab, cellular, and pile-supported raft (which combines both classes).

examTip.trick: A mat (raft) is a **shallow** foundation however large it is — the classification is by **load transfer**, not by size. It delivers load through its **base**, not by shaft friction.
examTip.mnemonic: **A raft SPREADS the load; piles TRANSFER it downward.** Different strategies for different problems — a raft does nothing to reach a deeper stratum, and piles do nothing to reduce the pressure near the surface.

questions.stem: The factor of safety for an infinite slope with steady seepage is:
options: Approximately half of the dry slope
questions.solution:
**Approximately half that of the dry slope.**

For an infinite slope in a **cohesionless** soil at angle β, the factor of safety takes a strikingly simple form:

**Dry slope (no seepage):**
> FoS = tan φ′ / tan β

**Steady seepage parallel to the slope, water table at the surface:**
> FoS = (γ′/γ_{sat}) × (tan φ′ / tan β)

So seepage multiplies the dry factor of safety by the ratio γ′/γ_{sat}.

**Putting numbers to it.** With typical values γ_{sat} ≈ 20 kN/m³ and γ_{w} = 9.81 kN/m³:
> γ′ = 20 − 9.81 = 10.19 kN/m³
> γ′/γ_{sat} = 10.19/20 ≈ **0.51**

The factor of safety is therefore **almost exactly halved** — which is the result the question is after.

**Why.** Seepage does two damaging things at once. The pore water pressure reduces the effective stress on the potential failure plane, cutting the frictional resistance; and the seepage force acting down the slope adds to the driving component. Both work in the same direction, and together they roughly halve the margin of safety.

**The engineering consequence** is the important part: a slope that stands perfectly well through the dry season can fail during prolonged monsoon rain with no change whatever to its geometry or its soil. This is the mechanism behind the great majority of **monsoon landslides in Nepal's hill roads**, and it is why slope stabilisation is fundamentally an exercise in **drainage** — surface drains, cut-off drains, sub-surface drains and weep holes — rather than only in retaining structures.

Note also that for a cohesionless infinite slope the factor of safety is **independent of depth**: it depends only on φ′ and β, so the slope is equally at risk at any depth, and the critical dry slope angle is simply β = φ′.

examTip.trick: For an infinite slope in cohesionless soil, **dry: F = tan φ/tan β**; with **steady seepage parallel to the slope: F = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β)**. Since γ′/γ_sat ≈ 10/20 = **0.5**, the factor of safety is roughly halved.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seepage HALVES the factor of safety of a sand slope** — which is precisely why slopes fail in the monsoon and stand all dry season. It is also why **drainage is the cheapest and most effective slope stabilisation measure** there is.

questions.stem: The bearing capacity of a square footing is:
questions.solution:
**q_u = 1.3cN_c + γDN_q + 0.4γBN_γ.**

Terzaghi derived his bearing capacity equation for a **strip** footing, then applied empirical shape factors to the cohesion and the width terms for other plan shapes. The **surcharge** term γDN_q is unaffected by shape.

The three standard forms, which must be kept apart:

| Footing | Ultimate bearing capacity |
|---|---|
| **Strip (continuous)** | q_u = **c**N_c + γDN_q + **0.5**γBN_γ |
| **Square** | q_u = **1.3c**N_c + γDN_q + **0.4**γBN_γ |
| **Circular** | q_u = **1.3c**N_c + γDN_q + **0.3**γBN_γ |

So the pattern to memorise is the pair of coefficients: **strip 1.0 and 0.5; square 1.3 and 0.4; circular 1.3 and 0.3.** Square and circular share the 1.3 on cohesion and differ only in the width term, which is why options (b) and (c) sit next to each other as the intended trap.

For a **rectangular** footing of length L and breadth B the shape factors interpolate:
> q_u = c N_c (1 + 0.3B/L) + γDN_q + 0.5γBN_γ (1 − 0.2B/L)

which correctly reduces to the strip case as B/L → 0.

Related facts examined alongside this:
- For **φ = 0** (saturated clay, undrained), N_c = **5.7**, N_q = 1, N_γ = 0, so a square footing gives q_u = 1.3 × 5.7c + γD = 7.4c + γD.
- **Net** ultimate bearing capacity q_{nu} = q_u − γD, and the **safe** bearing capacity is q_{nu}/FoS + γD with a factor of safety of 2.5 to 3.
- The **allowable** bearing pressure is the lesser of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by permissible settlement — in clay, settlement usually governs.

examTip.trick: The shape factors move in **opposite directions**: the cohesion term is **increased** to 1.3, while the width term is **reduced** to 0.4 (from 0.5).
examTip.mnemonic: **Square: 1.3 c N_c and 0.4 γBN_γ. Circular: 1.3 and 0.3. Strip: 1.0 and 0.5.** The opposite directions are geometric — a square footing's failure surface is confined on four sides (helping cohesion) but its wedge is smaller relative to its width (reducing the self-weight term).

questions.stem: Virtual work refers to:
options: Virtual work done by virtual forces
Virtual work done by actual forces
Actual work done by actual forces
Actual work done by virtual forces
questions.solution:
**Virtual work done by actual forces** — real forces moving through an imagined displacement.

The two words in "virtual work" attach to different things, which is exactly what the question probes:
- The **forces are real** — the actual loads and reactions on the structure.
- The **displacement is virtual** — a small, imaginary movement that we impose only as a mathematical device. It never actually happens.

The work computed from a real force acting through an imaginary displacement is therefore **virtual** work, done by **actual** forces.

**Principle of virtual work.** For a body in equilibrium, the total virtual work done by all the forces during any small virtual displacement consistent with the constraints is **zero**:

> Σ (F · δ) = 0

The virtual displacement must be **kinematically admissible** — it has to satisfy the support conditions and the continuity of the structure. Choosing it cleverly is the whole art of the method: release the one restraint whose force you want, let the structure move, and the equation yields that force directly without needing any of the others.

**Why it is powerful.** It converts a problem in equilibrium into a problem in geometry. It finds a single unknown reaction or member force in one step, and it underpins the **unit load method** for deflections, where a unit virtual load is applied at the point whose displacement is wanted:

> δ = ∫ (Mm/EI) dx  for bending, or Σ(Pu L/AE) for trusses

where M and P are the real internal actions and m and u those due to the unit virtual load.

Note the companion theorem: **Castigliano's** approach differs in using real strain energy and partial derivatives, whereas virtual work uses an imagined displacement — the two are related but not the same.

examTip.trap: The two virtual-work forms are easily reversed. **Virtual displacement** applies a fictitious displacement to real forces; **virtual force** applies a fictitious unit load to real displacements.
examTip.trick: Virtual work means the work done by the **actual force system** moving through a **compatible virtual displacement** — the forces are real, the displacement is imagined.
examTip.mnemonic: **The UNIT LOAD method is the everyday application** — apply a virtual unit load at the point and in the direction of the deflection you want, and δ = Σ(PkL/AE) for a truss or ∫(Mm/EI)dx for a beam.

questions.stem: The deflection at the centre of a fixed beam with total load W applied uniformly over its length L is:
questions.solution:
**WL³/384EI.**

Both forms of this result are in circulation and the difference is only in how the load is expressed:

> In terms of **total** load W: δ = **WL³/(384EI)**
> In terms of load **intensity** w (so W = wL): δ = wL⁴/(384EI)

The question gives the **total load W**, so the exponent on L is **3**, and the answer is (b).

**Dimensional check — the fastest way to eliminate options.** Deflection must have the dimension of length:
> W [N] × L³ [m³] ÷ (E [N/m²] × I [m⁴]) = m ✓

whereas WL⁴/EI would give m², which is not a length. That single test kills options (a) and (c) immediately, leaving only a choice between the 384 and 192 denominators.

The standard deflection results, worth holding as a table since the denominators are what get confused:

| Beam and loading | Central deflection (total load W) |
|---|---|
| Simply supported, central point load | WL³/**48**EI |
| Simply supported, UDL | 5WL³/**384**EI |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL** | **WL³/384EI** |
| Fixed both ends, central point load | WL³/**192**EI |
| Cantilever, end point load | WL³/**3**EI |
| Cantilever, UDL | WL³/**8**EI |

Note the neat relationship: fixing the ends of a UDL-loaded beam reduces the deflection to **one fifth** of the simply supported value (384 against 5/384 — that is, 5×). The end moments generated by the fixity bend the beam back, and that is the structural value of continuity.

Option (d), WL³/192EI, is the fixed beam with a **central point load** — the other fixed-beam case, and the intended distractor here.

examTip.trick: Compare the three UDL deflections directly: **simply supported 5WL³/384EI**, **fixed both ends WL³/384EI**, **propped cantilever WL³/185EI** (in terms of total load W = wL).
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixing both ends cuts the deflection to ONE FIFTH and the peak moment by a third** (wL²/8 → wL²/12). That is why continuity is so structurally valuable — and why the price, sensitivity to support settlement, has to be accepted.

questions.stem: According to NRRS, an arterial road is called:
questions.solution:
**Path**, according to the hierarchy given in the source answer key.

The Nepali functional names, as the source sets them out:

| Nepali term | Function |
|---|---|
| **Path** | **Arterial road** — through traffic on a continuous route; highest order |
| Sadak | Sub-arterial road — lower mobility; links arterials to district headquarters |
| Marga | Collector road — collects and distributes traffic to and from local roads |
| Upamarga | Local road — access to individual properties |

On that reading, an arterial road is a **Path**, and the answer is (a).

The underlying functional classification is the part worth learning regardless of the naming, because it is universal:
- **Arterial** — mobility is the priority; access is restricted; long, continuous routes carrying through traffic.
- **Sub-arterial** — still mobility-oriented but shorter and with more access points.
- **Collector** — balances mobility and access; gathers traffic from local roads and feeds it to the arterials.
- **Local** — access is the priority, mobility is incidental; serves individual plots.

Separately, Nepal's **functional classification for the national network** (Nepal Road Standard) is the one more commonly examined: **National Highway (H), Feeder Road (F), District Road (D) and Urban Road (U)** — the subject of Set 1 Q97.

**Flagged for verification.** This ordering is taken from the source answer key and could not be confirmed against the published Nepal Rural Road Standard. It runs counter to ordinary Nepali usage, in which *path* generally denotes a minor lane or trail and *marga* a major road — so the hierarchy above may be inverted. Treat the functional definitions as reliable and the Nepali labels as provisional until checked against the current NRRS document.

verification.notes: The keyed answer (a) is retained because the source explanation states the hierarchy explicitly, but it could not be independently verified. Ordinary Nepali usage suggests the opposite ordering (path = lane/trail, marga = major road), so the naming may be inverted in the source. The functional definitions of arterial/sub-arterial/collector/local are standard and reliable; only the Nepali labels are in doubt. Owner should confirm against the published NRRS before this question is used in a paid set.

examTip.trick: Road classifications differ between **function** (arterial, sub-arterial, collector, local) and **administration** (national highway, feeder, district, urban). The question asks for the NRRS term.
examTip.mnemonic: **Function describes what the road DOES — mobility versus access.** An arterial maximises mobility with restricted access; a local street is the reverse. Every road sits somewhere on that continuum, and mixing the two roles is what makes a road both congested and dangerous.

questions.stem: Seasoning of timber is done:
questions.solution:
**To remove water** — that is, to reduce the moisture content to a level in equilibrium with the atmosphere in which the timber will be used.

Freshly felled green timber may carry a moisture content well above 50%. As it dries in service it **shrinks**, and because shrinkage is unequal along, across and radially through the grain, the member **warps, twists, cups and splits**. Seasoning removes that water *before* the timber is worked and fixed, so the shrinkage happens under control rather than in the finished structure.

The benefits that follow:
- **Dimensional stability** — no further significant shrinkage or warping in service.
- **Higher strength and stiffness** — dry timber is considerably stronger than green timber.
- **Resistance to decay** — fungi and most insects need moisture above about 20% to attack timber.
- Lower weight, easier working, and it will now **hold paint, polish and preservative**, which green timber will not.

Note that the last point disposes of options (a) and (b): seasoning makes timber *fit to be painted or treated*, but it does not itself waterproof or paint the wood.

**Target moisture content** is about **10 to 12%** for interior joinery and **15 to 18%** for exterior work — matched to the humidity where the timber will sit.

The methods:

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Natural (air) seasoning** | Stacked under cover with spacers for free air movement. Cheap, no equipment, but **slow** — months to years — and cannot go below ambient humidity |
| **Kiln seasoning** | Controlled temperature and humidity in a chamber. **Fast** (days to weeks), reaches any target moisture content, and kills insects and fungi. Needs plant and skill; too rapid a schedule causes surface checking |
| Water, boiling, chemical, electrical seasoning | Special-purpose accelerated methods |

examTip.trap: "To increase strength" is a **consequence**, not the purpose — and choosing it means missing that every other benefit follows from moisture removal too.
examTip.trick: One cause, many effects: lower moisture gives **less shrinkage and warping, greater strength, better paint and glue adhesion, and resistance to decay and insect attack**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Season to about 12% for interior work, 15–18% for exterior.** Methods ranked by speed against damage: **air** (slow, gentle), **kiln** (fast, controlled), **electrical and chemical** (quick, harsh, expensive). Fast seasoning sets up a moisture gradient, and the gradient splits the timber.

questions.stem: The ratio of the volume of water present in a given soil mass to the total volume of its voids is known as:
questions.solution:
**Degree of saturation.**

> S = V_{w} / V_{v} × 100%

The denominator is what identifies it: the ratio is taken against the **volume of voids**, so it measures how full the pore space is. S = 0 for perfectly dry soil and **S = 100% for fully saturated soil**, where every void is occupied by water.

The volumetric relationships, which differ only in what sits above and below the line — and that is exactly what this question tests:

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Degree of saturation, S** | **V_water / V_voids** |
| Void ratio, e | V_voids / V_solids |
| Porosity, n | V_voids / V_total |
| Percentage air voids, n_a | V_air / V_total |
| Air content, a_c | V_air / V_voids |
| Water content, w | **W_water / W_solids** (a *weight* ratio, not volumetric) |

Note the two easy traps: **porosity** uses total volume in the denominator, not void volume; and **water content** is a ratio of *weights*, so it can exceed 100% in a soft organic clay, whereas the degree of saturation never can.

The relations that tie them together, and are needed constantly in numericals:

> **e = n/(1 − n)**  and  **n = e/(1 + e)**
> **S·e = w·G_{s}** — the single most useful identity in soil phase problems
> γ = γ_{w}(G_{s} + Se)/(1 + e)

The identity **Se = wG_s** is worth committing outright: given any three of S, e, w and G_s it delivers the fourth, and it is how Set 2 Q78 (the pycnometer problem) is solved.

examTip.trap: **Water content** is the near-miss and is defined on **weights of water and solids**, not on volumes of water and voids. Read whether the ratio is of volumes or of weights.
examTip.trick: **S = V_w/V_v** — a fraction of the **VOID** volume, so it runs from 0 (dry) to 1 (fully saturated) and can never exceed 1.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water content w = W_w/W_s can exceed 100%** (soft marine clays reach 200%); **degree of saturation S never can.** The link between them is **eS = wG**, which solves most phase problems on its own.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the shear stress distribution in circular pipes with laminar flow?
options: It is linear with maximum value at the centre
It is parabolic with maximum value at the centre
It is parabolic with zero value at the centre
It is linear with zero value at the centre
questions.solution:
**Linear, with zero value at the centre.**

This is the classic pairing that candidates invert. In fully developed laminar flow through a circular pipe:

| Quantity | Distribution | At centre | At wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shear stress** | **Linear** in r | **Zero** | **Maximum** |
| **Velocity** | **Parabolic** in r | **Maximum** | Zero |

**Shear stress** — from a force balance on a cylindrical element of radius r:
> τ = (Δp/2L) · r

τ is directly proportional to r, hence **linear**, rising from zero on the axis to τ_{0} at the wall.

**Velocity** — integrating τ = μ(du/dr) gives
> u = (Δp/4μL)(R² − r²)

which is **parabolic**, with u_{max} at the axis. The mean velocity is exactly half the maximum, V = u_{max}/2.

**Why shear is zero at the centre.** On the axis the flow is symmetric — there is no velocity gradient there, since the velocity profile has a smooth maximum and du/dr = 0. No gradient means no shear stress. At the wall the gradient is steepest, so the shear is greatest, which is exactly why friction loss is a wall phenomenon.

The options are constructed to catch the swap: (b) "parabolic with maximum at the centre" is the **velocity** profile, offered as though it described shear stress.

Related laminar-flow results:
> **Hagen–Poiseuille:** Q = πΔpD⁴/(128μL), so head loss h_{f} = 32μVL/(γD²) — proportional to **V**, not V²
> f = **64/Re** for laminar flow
> Laminar flow holds for **Re < 2000**; turbulent above about 4000

examTip.trick: Force balance on a cylindrical element gives **τ = (Δp/2L)r**, so the shear varies **linearly from τ₀ at the wall to ZERO at the centreline** — and this holds in **both** laminar and turbulent flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear distribution is linear in BOTH regimes; only the VELOCITY profile differs** (parabolic laminar, logarithmic turbulent). Note the shear is maximum at the wall, not zero — a common reversal.

questions.stem: In influence line diagrams (ILD):
options: Points remain fixed, position of load changes
Points change, position of loads remain fixed
questions.solution:
**The point remains fixed and the position of the load changes.**

This is the defining distinction between an influence line and an ordinary bending moment or shear force diagram, and it is worth being completely clear about:

| | **Influence line diagram** | **BM / SF diagram** |
|---|---|---|
| Section considered | **One fixed point** | **Every section** along the beam |
| Load | A **unit load moving** across the span | Fixed in position |
| Ordinate means | The value of the function at *that one point* when the unit load is at *this* position | The value of the function *at this section* for the given fixed loading |

So an ILD answers: *"for the response at section C, where should the load be to make it large?"* An ordinary BM diagram answers: *"for this loading, where is the beam most heavily stressed?"* One varies the load position; the other varies the section.

**Why it is indispensable.** For moving loads — a train of wheels crossing a bridge girder, a crane travelling along a gantry — the critical loading position is not obvious. The influence line makes it obvious by construction: place the loads over the **largest ordinates** of the appropriate sign, and the response is maximised.

**Muller-Breslau principle** gives a shortcut: the shape of the influence line for any reaction, shear or moment is the deflected shape of the structure when the corresponding restraint is released and a unit displacement is imposed at that release.

The standard results for a simply supported beam of span L, with the section at distance a from A (b = L − a):

| Function | Peak ordinate | At |
|---|---|---|
| Reaction R_{A} | 1.0 | Support A |
| **Bending moment at C** | **ab/L** | At the section C |
| Shear at C | b/L and −a/L | Just each side of C |

The practical rules that follow — trailing load at a support for maximum shear (Q7 of this paper) and maximum moment always under a wheel load (Set 1 Q5) — are both read straight off these diagrams.

examTip.trap: It is constantly confused with a bending moment diagram, where the **section** varies and the **load** is fixed. An influence line is the exact reverse.
examTip.trick: One quantity, **one fixed section**, and the **unit load moves**. The horizontal axis is the position of the **load**, not a position on the beam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load → put it at the maximum ordinate. UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.** Because a shear influence line changes sign at the section, maximum shear comes from loading **one side only** — which is exactly the pattern-loading principle for continuous beams.

questions.stem: With a percentage increase of carbon in steel, it decreases its:
questions.solution:
**Ductility.**

Carbon is the single most influential element in steel, and raising its content pushes every property in a consistent direction:

| Property | Effect of increasing carbon |
|---|---|
| Strength (tensile, yield) | **Increases** |
| Hardness | **Increases** |
| Brittleness | **Increases** |
| **Ductility** | **Decreases** |
| Toughness (impact resistance) | Decreases |
| **Weldability** | **Decreases** |
| Melting point | Decreases |

So three of the four options increase, and only **ductility** falls — which makes the question a test of whether the candidate has the direction of the trade-off firmly in mind.

The mechanism: carbon forms hard, brittle **iron carbide (cementite, Fe₃C)** within the softer ferrite matrix. The carbide particles obstruct the movement of dislocations, so the metal resists deformation more strongly — it is harder and stronger — but for the same reason it can no longer deform plastically before fracturing.

Classification by carbon content:

| Steel | Carbon | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Wrought iron | < 0.05% | Very soft and ductile |
| **Mild (low carbon)** | **0.05 – 0.25%** | **Ductile, weldable — structural steel, rebar** |
| Medium carbon | 0.25 – 0.6% | Rails, shafts, forgings |
| High carbon | 0.6 – 1.5% | Springs, tools, cutting edges |
| Cast iron | 2 – 4% | Hard, brittle, good in compression only |

**Why this matters in civil engineering.** Structural steel and reinforcement are deliberately kept to the **low-carbon** range: a structure must be able to deform and warn before it fails, and it must be weldable on site. That is the same trade-off seen in the rebar grades — Fe 250 gives 23% elongation, Fe 500 only 12%, and Fe 550 just 10% — which is why seismic codes call for **Fe 500D** with its enhanced ductility rather than plain Fe 500.

examTip.trick: More carbon means **harder and stronger** but **less ductile, less tough and less weldable**. Every desirable property does not move the same way.
examTip.mnemonic: **Carbon up: hardness and strength UP; ductility, toughness and weldability DOWN.** That trade-off is why structural steel is kept at **0.15–0.25% carbon** — high-carbon steel would be stronger but could not be welded or bent, and would fail without warning.

questions.stem: Alum is chemically:
questions.solution:
**Aluminium sulphate**, Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O — the standard coagulant in water treatment.

**How it works.** Added to raw water, alum hydrolyses and produces insoluble **aluminium hydroxide** floc while releasing acid:

> Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O + 3Ca(HCO₃)₂ → 2Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CaSO₄ + 6CO₂ + 18H₂O

The gelatinous Al(OH)₃ floc neutralises the negative surface charge on colloidal clay and organic particles, letting them collide and agglomerate into flocs large enough to settle. Colloids would otherwise stay in suspension indefinitely, since their electrostatic repulsion prevents them from coming together.

**Operating conditions worth knowing:**
- Effective **pH range 6.5 to 8.5**, optimum about 7.
- Dose typically **10 to 40 mg/L**, fixed by a laboratory **jar test** rather than by formula.
- **Alkalinity is consumed** — about 0.5 mg/L as CaCO₃ per mg/L of alum. Soft or low-alkalinity water needs lime or soda ash added, or the pH will fall out of the effective range and coagulation will fail.

The treatment sequence in which it sits: **rapid mixing (flash mix) → flocculation (slow stirring, 20–40 min) → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection.**

The alternative coagulants, which the distractors name:

| Coagulant | Note |
|---|---|
| **Alum — aluminium sulphate** | **Most common; cheap and effective** |
| Ferrous sulphate (copperas) | Needs lime; works over a wider pH range |
| Ferric chloride / ferric sulphate | Effective at wider pH; more corrosive to handle |
| Sodium aluminate | Used for soft water; adds alkalinity |
| Polyaluminium chloride (PAC) | Modern; lower dose, less alkalinity consumed |

Note that **copper sulphate** (option a) is not a coagulant at all — it is dosed into reservoirs as an **algicide**.

examTip.trick: **Al₂(SO₄)₃** — aluminium sulphate, the standard coagulant. In water it forms **aluminium hydroxide floc** that sweeps up colloidal particles.
examTip.mnemonic: **Alum works best at pH 6.5–8.5, and it CONSUMES ALKALINITY** — so soft, low-alkalinity water needs lime added or the pH crashes and coagulation fails. Typical dose 10–50 mg/l. Rapid mix first (seconds), then slow flocculation (20–40 min) to grow the floc.

questions.stem: Bligh's theory of seepage assumes:
options: Equal weightage to the horizontal and vertical creep
More weightage to horizontal creep than vertical creep
Less weightage to horizontal creep than vertical creep
Loss of head follows the sine curve
questions.solution:
**Equal weightage to horizontal and vertical creep.**

Bligh's **creep theory** (1910) makes the simplest possible assumption about water percolating beneath a hydraulic structure: the water "creeps" along the contact surface of the base profile, and **every millimetre of that path is equally effective in dissipating head**, whether the water is travelling horizontally along the floor or vertically down a cut-off.

So the creep length is just the sum of all the segments:
> L = b + 2d₁ + 2d₂ + 2d₃ + …

and the head is assumed to be lost **uniformly** along it, giving a hydraulic gradient

> H/L = 1/C

where C is **Bligh's coefficient of creep**, taken as 12 for coarse gravel, 15 for coarse sand, and up to 18 for fine micaceous sand. The safety requirement is that the creep length provided must be at least **C × H**.

**Why the assumption is wrong.** Khosla's investigations showed that the equipotential lines do not distribute head uniformly, and that **vertical cut-offs are far more effective than horizontal floor length** in reducing the exit gradient. Bligh's theory therefore over-values horizontal creep and under-values vertical creep, and it also gives no way of finding the **exit gradient**, which is the quantity that actually governs piping failure.

| | **Bligh's creep theory** | **Khosla's theory** |
|---|---|---|
| Head loss | **Uniform** along the creep path | Non-uniform; from potential flow theory |
| Horizontal vs vertical creep | **Equally weighted** | **Vertical much more effective** |
| Basis | Empirical | **Flow net / conformal mapping**, with correction factors |
| Gives exit gradient? | No | **Yes** — G_{E} = (H/d)(1/π√λ) |
| Status | Superseded | **Current design practice** |

Option (d) refers to Lane's weighted creep theory and to the general shape of the potential distribution, not to Bligh's assumption. Lane's method sits between the two, weighting vertical creep three times as heavily as horizontal.

examTip.trap: Bligh's assumption is precisely what makes it **wrong**, and structures designed on it have failed. The question is testing whether you know its defect.
examTip.trick: Bligh's **creep theory** treats vertical and horizontal seepage paths as **equally effective**. They are not — a **vertical cut-off is far more effective per metre** than horizontal floor length.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh counted length; Lane weighted vertical creep three times horizontal; KHOSLA solved the actual flow.** Khosla showed the safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT** and on the **downstream cut-off**, not on total creep length.

questions.stem: Penstock in a hydroelectric power plant is:
options: A pipe connected to runner outlet
Nozzle that releases high pressure water on turbine blades
A conduit connecting forebay to the scroll case of turbine
A pipe connecting surge tank to dam
questions.solution:
**A conduit connecting the forebay to the scroll case of the turbine.**

The penstock is the **high-pressure pipe** that carries water from the forebay (or from the surge tank) down to the turbine, converting the available head into pressure at the machine. It is usually steel, sometimes concrete-lined or embedded, and is the most highly stressed component of the waterway.

Trace the full water route through a run-of-river plant, since the question is really testing whether the candidate can place the component in sequence:

> **Intake → settling basin → headrace tunnel or canal → forebay → surge tank → penstock → turbine (scroll case → runner) → draft tube → tailrace**

Why the other options name different components:

| Option | Actually describes |
|---|---|
| Pipe at runner outlet | **Draft tube** — recovers residual kinetic energy in a reaction turbine |
| Nozzle releasing high pressure water on the blades | **Nozzle of a Pelton wheel** — converts pressure head to a free jet |
| **Conduit from forebay to scroll case** | **Penstock** ✓ |
| Pipe from surge tank to dam | The headrace conduit lies on the other side of the surge tank |

Design considerations examined alongside:
- **Economic diameter** balances the capital cost of a larger pipe against the lifetime value of head lost to friction in a smaller one.
- Thickness is governed by internal pressure **including the water-hammer rise**, from the hoop stress relation t = pD/(2σ).
- **Anchor blocks** resist the thrust at bends, and expansion joints accommodate temperature movement.
- **Surge protection** — a surge tank at the upper end, as in Q30 of this paper — limits the water-hammer pressure to the penstock length below it.
- A **forebay** provides a small balancing storage and a final chance for sediment to settle before water enters the penstock.

examTip.trick: Trace the water's path: **intake → headrace (canal or tunnel) → forebay or surge tank → PENSTOCK → turbine → tailrace**. The penstock is the steep pressure pipe that converts head into velocity at the machine.
examTip.mnemonic: **The penstock is the high-pressure member and must be designed for static head PLUS water hammer surge** — which can double or triple the static value. Above it, the surge tank protects the low-pressure headrace; below it, nothing does.

questions.stem: The relationship between SSD and ISD is:
questions.solution:
**Option (d)** — the option expressing a factor-of-two relationship between the two distances.

The engineering relation is that **intersection sight distance is twice the stopping sight distance**:

> **ISD = 2 × SSD**

A driver approaching an uncontrolled intersection needs more than the distance to stop for an object ahead. They must see a vehicle approaching on the crossing road, judge its speed, decide whether to proceed or yield, and then either clear the intersection or come to a halt. Two independent vehicles are manoeuvring, so roughly twice the stopping distance is required — hence the factor of two, and why IRC bases the sight triangle at an intersection on this multiple.

For reference:
> SSD = lag distance + braking distance = **vt + v²/(2gf)**, with reaction time t = 2.5 s

**A note on the printed options.** Option (d) as printed reads "SSD = 2 ISD", which inverts the relation — it would make the stopping distance the larger of the two, which is not the case. Option (b), "SSD = 1.5 SSD", is self-referential and meaningless, so it is plainly a typesetting error as well. Option (d) is nonetheless the intended answer, being the only choice that expresses the 2 : 1 relationship the question is testing. Read it as **ISD = 2 SSD**.

The three sight distances, to keep the hierarchy straight:

| Sight distance | Requirement | Magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **SSD** | Stop safely for an object in the path | Smallest; provided everywhere |
| **ISD** | See and negotiate a crossing vehicle | **≈ 2 × SSD** |
| **OSD** | Complete an overtaking manoeuvre on a two-lane two-way road | Largest; ≈ 14.4 v (v in km/h) |

On a **two-way single-lane** road the sight distance provided must also be twice the SSD, since both approaching vehicles have to stop.

verification.notes: The printed option (d) reads 'SSD = 2 ISD', which inverts the correct relation ISD = 2 SSD; option (b) 'SSD = 1.5 SSD' is self-referential and also a typesetting error. Option (d) is retained as the keyed answer since it is the only choice expressing the 2:1 relationship being tested, and the solution states the correct direction explicitly.

examTip.trap: The relation is easy to invert. **ISD = 2 × SSD**, so **SSD = ISD/2** — the intermediate sight distance is the LONGER of the two.
examTip.trick: ISD is provided where full **overtaking** sight distance cannot be achieved but something better than bare stopping distance is wanted — so it must be longer than SSD.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ladder of sight distances: SSD < ISD (= 2 SSD) < OSD.** SSD is the absolute minimum and must be available on every metre of road; OSD is provided where economically possible on two-lane roads.

questions.stem: Enoscope is used to determine:
questions.solution:
**Spot speed.**

An **enoscope** (or mirror box) is a simple L-shaped tube with a mirror set at 45°. Placed at the roadside, it lets an observer standing at one end of a short measured base see the vehicle cross the far reference line at right angles to the road, without having to look along the carriageway. The time taken to cover the known short base is measured with a stopwatch, and

> spot speed = base length / time

The base is typically **30 m**, short enough that the vehicle's speed does not change appreciably over it — which is what makes the result a *spot* speed, the instantaneous speed at a particular point.

The methods of measuring spot speed, in order of sophistication:

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Enoscope** | **Simple, cheap, manual; needs a short measured base** |
| Pressure contact tube / pneumatic tube | Two tubes across the road, time between pulses |
| **Radar speedmeter** | Doppler shift; instantaneous, no base needed, widely used for enforcement |
| Photographic / video, and modern loop detectors | Automatic, large samples |

Why the other options are wrong: **average speed** over a length and **travel time** are measured by quite different techniques — the license-plate method, the floating-car (moving observer) method, or GPS tracking — because they concern behaviour over a route, not at a point.

What spot-speed data is used for, which is the reason the study is made at all: plotting the cumulative frequency curve and reading off the **85th percentile** for the speed limit, the **98th percentile** for geometric design, and the **15th percentile** for a minimum speed limit — the subject of Q26 of this paper.

Note also the distinction between **time mean speed** (the arithmetic average of individual spot speeds) and **space mean speed** (harmonic mean, obtained over a length). Space mean speed is always the lower of the two, and it is the one used in the fundamental traffic relation **q = k × v_s**.

examTip.trick: An enoscope is a simple **mirror box** that lets one observer see a vehicle crossing a distant line at right angles, so a single person can time it over a short base — a **spot speed** measurement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spot speed = speed at ONE point. Journey speed = distance ÷ total time INCLUDING stops. Running speed excludes stops.** Spot speed studies feed the **85th percentile** used to set speed limits.

questions.stem: The ratio obtained by dividing 'quick assets' by current liabilities is called:
questions.solution:
**Acid test ratio**, also called the **quick ratio**.

> Acid test ratio = **Quick assets / Current liabilities**

where **quick assets** are the current assets that can be turned into cash almost immediately — cash and bank balances, marketable securities and receivables — with **inventory and prepaid expenses excluded**.

That exclusion is the whole point of the ratio. Stock may take weeks to sell, and in a forced sale may fetch far less than its book value, so it is not a reliable source of cash for meeting an immediate obligation. Stripping it out gives a harsher, more honest measure of short-term liquidity — hence the name "acid test".

> A value of **1.0 or above** is generally regarded as satisfactory: the firm can meet its current liabilities without having to sell any inventory.

The liquidity and solvency ratios, which the options deliberately mix:

| Ratio | Formula | Measures | Healthy value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current ratio** | Current assets / Current liabilities | Short-term liquidity, inventory **included** | ≈ 2.0 |
| **Acid test (quick) ratio** | **Quick assets / Current liabilities** | Short-term liquidity, inventory **excluded** | **≈ 1.0** |
| Solvency ratio | Total assets / Total liabilities | **Long-term** ability to meet all debts | > 1.0 |
| Turnover ratio | Sales / Assets (or inventory) | **Efficiency** of asset use, not liquidity | Higher is better |

So the **current ratio** is the near miss — same denominator, but it includes inventory in the numerator. **Solvency** looks at the long term rather than the immediate, and **turnover** measures efficiency, not liquidity at all.

For a contractor these ratios matter directly: they are examined during **pre-qualification and tender evaluation** as evidence that the firm can fund the work and pay subcontractors and suppliers on time.

examTip.trick: **Quick (liquid) assets** exclude inventory, because stock cannot be turned into cash quickly. So the acid test is a harsher measure of short-term solvency than the current ratio.
examTip.mnemonic: **Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities (target ~2). Acid test = QUICK assets/current liabilities (target ~1).** The acid test asks: could the business pay its immediate debts without selling any stock?

questions.stem: In a non-parallel system of seismic design, 100% design seismic force of one direction and X% design seismic force of the orthogonal direction is considered. The value of X is:
questions.solution:
**30%.**

An earthquake does not arrive along a building's convenient axes. Where the lateral load resisting elements are **not oriented along two clean orthogonal directions** — a non-parallel system — a single member can be excited by ground motion from both directions at once, so the codes require the two directional effects to be combined:

> **± 100% of the force in one direction ± 30% of the force in the orthogonal direction**

and the same rule applied with the roles of the two directions reversed. Every sign combination must be checked, and the member is designed for the worst.

**Why 30% rather than 100%.** The peak responses in the two directions do not occur at the same instant. Adding both at full value would be excessively conservative; ignoring the second entirely would be unsafe. The 30% figure is the accepted compromise, derived from the statistics of the phase difference between the two components.

Related requirements from the same clause of the seismic codes:
- The **vertical** component is also combined at 30% where it matters — long cantilevers, prestressed members and horizontal projections.
- The rule applies whenever the structure has a **non-parallel system irregularity**, and also to buildings with **corner columns** in a regular frame, since those are common to both orthogonal frames.

This sits within the broader family of plan and vertical irregularities that trigger more demanding analysis: torsional irregularity, re-entrant corners, diaphragm discontinuity, out-of-plane offsets and **non-parallel systems** in plan; soft or weak storey, mass irregularity, geometric irregularity and in-plane discontinuity in elevation. A **soft storey** — the open ground floor so common in Nepali buildings — is the most dangerous of these, and was a major cause of collapse in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.

examTip.trick: Earthquake shaking has no preferred direction, so a structure must be checked for the **combination** of simultaneous orthogonal effects — the code convention being **100% in one direction plus 30% in the other**.
examTip.mnemonic: **100% + 30%, applied both ways round** (and with both signs) — so eight combinations. This matters most for **corner columns**, which receive significant demand from both directions at once and are frequently the critical members in a seismic design.

questions.stem: In a three hinged symmetric arch of span 40 m and central rise 8 m, an 80 kN point load is acting at a distance of 6 m from support A. Determine the horizontal thrust.
questions.solution:
**30 kN.**

A three-hinged arch is **statically determinate**, so no strain energy or compatibility is needed — only statics. The third hinge at the crown supplies the extra equation.

**Step 1 — vertical reactions.** Taking moments about B:
> V_{A} = 80 × (40 − 6)/40 = 80 × 34/40 = **68 kN**
> V_{B} = 80 × 6/40 = **12 kN**

Check: 68 + 12 = 80 ✓

**Step 2 — horizontal thrust from the crown hinge.** The crown C is a hinge, so it can carry no moment. Taking moments of all forces to the **left** of C about C (clockwise positive), with the crown at mid-span, 20 m from A, and 8 m above the springing:

> V_{A} × 20 − H × 8 − 80 × (20 − 6) = 0
> 68 × 20 − 8H − 80 × 14 = 0
> 1360 − 8H − 1120 = 0
> 8H = 240
> **H = 30 kN**

The general form is worth remembering: **H = M_{c}/y_{c}**, where M_{c} is the bending moment that a simply supported beam of the same span and loading would have at the crown section, and y_{c} is the rise. Here M_{c} = 1360 − 1120 = 240 kN·m and y_{c} = 8 m, giving H = 240/8 = 30 kN directly.

That relation also shows why arches are efficient: the **thrust is inversely proportional to the rise**. A shallow arch develops enormous horizontal thrust, which the abutments must resist — the reason flat arches need massive foundations or tie rods.

**A note on the printed question.** The original describes the arch as "semicircular" while giving a span of 40 m with a central rise of only 8 m. Those are geometrically incompatible — a true semicircular arch of 40 m span has a rise of 20 m. The word has been omitted here, since the intended calculation (and the keyed answer) uses the stated rise of 8 m, and the crown-moment method above does not depend on the shape of the arch axis in any case.

verification.notes: The printed stem says 'semicircular' with span 40 m and central rise 8 m, which is impossible (a semicircular arch of 40 m span rises 20 m). The source's own working uses the stated rise of 8 m, giving H = 30 kN. The inconsistent word has been dropped from the stem; the calculation and answer are unaffected.

examTip.trick: A **three-hinged arch is DETERMINATE**. Find the vertical reactions by moments about the supports, then get the horizontal thrust by taking **moments about the crown hinge**, where the moment must be zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **H = M_crown(as a simple beam)/rise.** The crown hinge is what makes the whole problem solvable by statics — and it is also why three-hinged arches are used where **settlement or temperature movement** is expected: being determinate, they develop no self-stress.

questions.stem: If the rate of interest is 4% for the first year, 5% for the second year and 6% for the third year, then the compound interest on ₹10,000 for 3 years, if interest is compounded annually, is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 1575.20.**

With a rate that changes each year, the single-rate formula F = P(1 + i)ⁿ cannot be used. Instead apply each year's rate to the balance carried forward:

> F = P(1 + i₁)(1 + i₂)(1 + i₃)

**Year by year:**
> End of year 1: 10 000 × 1.04 = **Rs 10 400**
> End of year 2: 10 400 × 1.05 = **Rs 10 920**
> End of year 3: 10 920 × 1.06 = **Rs 11 575.20**

**Compound interest** is the amount earned over and above the principal:
> CI = 11 575.20 − 10 000 = **Rs 1 575.20**

The question asks for the **interest**, not the final amount — a distinction worth pausing on, since misreading it is the commonest error in this type of problem.

**A useful check.** Simple interest at the same three rates would be 10 000 × (0.04 + 0.05 + 0.06) = Rs 1 500 — which is exactly option (c). Compound interest must always **exceed** simple interest, because interest earns interest, so any answer at or below 1 500 can be discarded at once. That single observation eliminates (c) and confirms the answer must be a little above it.

Note also that the **order of the rates does not matter**: multiplication is commutative, so 4-5-6 gives the same final amount as 6-5-4. Only the set of rates matters, not the sequence.

The equivalent single rate over the three years would satisfy (1 + i)³ = 1.04 × 1.05 × 1.06 = 1.15752, giving **i ≈ 4.997%** — very close to, but not exactly, the arithmetic mean of 5%.

examTip.trick: With a **changing** interest rate the factors **multiply** in sequence — you cannot average the rates. **F = P(1.04)(1.05)(1.06)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compound each year at its own rate, in order.** Averaging the rates and compounding three times gives a slightly different (wrong) answer, and the error grows with the spread between the rates.

questions.stem: What is the formula for shear strength from the vane shear test?
questions.solution:
**S = T / [πD²(H/2 + D/6)].**

The vane shear test measures the **undrained shear strength** of a soft, saturated, cohesive soil *in situ*. A four-bladed vane of diameter D and height H is pushed into the soil and rotated; the torque T at failure is measured with a calibrated spring.

**Where the formula comes from.** At failure the soil shears over a cylindrical surface, and resistance is mobilised on three surfaces at once:
- the **curved side** of the cylinder, contributing a moment involving H;
- the **top and bottom** circular faces, each contributing a moment involving D.

Summing those moments and equating to the applied torque gives

> T = πD²S (H/2 + D/6)  ⟹  **S = T / [πD²(H/2 + D/6)]**

The H/2 term is the side contribution and the D/6 term the two end faces. Where only one end shears — a vane rotated at the bottom of a borehole with the top face not embedded — the end term becomes D/12 instead.

**How T is obtained:** T = (spring constant / 180) × (initial reading − final reading), reading the torsion spring deflection in degrees.

**Why the test matters.** It is the standard field method for soft clay where sampling would disturb the soil beyond usefulness. It gives c_{u} directly with **φ = 0**, and — importantly — it can be repeated after the vane has been rotated several turns to measure the **remoulded** strength, so the test yields the **sensitivity**:

> Sensitivity = undisturbed strength / remoulded strength

A sensitivity above about 8 marks a *quick* clay, which loses almost all its strength on disturbance — a serious hazard in excavation and pile driving.

The test is suitable only for **soft to medium clays** with c_{u} below about 100 kPa; stiff clay, or any soil containing sand, gravel or fibrous peat, will jam or shear irregularly and invalidate the result.

examTip.trick: The torque is resisted by shear on the **cylindrical side surface** (the πD²H/2 term) plus the **two circular ends** (the πD³/6 term). Adding them and rearranging gives the formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **The vane's great advantage is that the clay is NEVER SAMPLED, transported or trimmed** — which is exactly what a sensitive clay cannot survive. Turning the vane on past failure also gives the **remoulded** strength, so one test yields the **sensitivity** directly.

questions.stem: If the depression in a glass tube of 1.2 mm diameter immersed in mercury is 8 mm, then find the diameter of tube to have a depression of 4 mm.
questions.solution:
**2.4 mm.**

Capillary rise or depression:

> h = 4σ cos θ / (ρgd)

Everything except h and d is fixed — same liquid (mercury), same tube material, so σ, θ and ρ are unchanged. Therefore

> **h ∝ 1/d**, or equivalently **h · d = constant**

**Applying it:**
> h₁d₁ = h₂d₂
> 8 × 1.2 = 4 × d₂
> 9.6 = 4d₂
> **d₂ = 2.4 mm**

So **halving the depression requires doubling the diameter** — the inverse proportionality in its simplest form. Recognising that relationship turns this from an algebra exercise into a one-line calculation; there is no need to know σ or θ at all.

**Why mercury depresses rather than rises.** For mercury against glass the contact angle is about **130°–140°**, so cos θ is **negative** and h comes out negative — a depression. Water against glass has θ ≈ 0°, cos θ = +1, and it rises. The physical cause is whether the liquid–solid adhesion exceeds the liquid's own cohesion: water wets glass, mercury does not.

| Liquid in glass | Contact angle | Meniscus | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water** | ≈ 0° | Concave up | **Rise** |
| **Mercury** | ≈ 130–140° | Convex up | **Depression** |

**The practical consequence** of h ∝ 1/d: capillary error is significant in narrow tubes and negligible in wide ones. Manometer and piezometer tubes are therefore kept above about **6 mm** bore so the correction can be ignored — and the same inverse-diameter law governs capillary rise in soils, where it explains why fine-grained silts draw water far higher than coarse sands.

examTip.trick: Capillary rise or depression is **inversely proportional to diameter**: **h ∝ 1/d**. Multiplying the diameter by 1.2/0.6... here the tube diameter changes, so scale the depression by the inverse ratio.
examTip.mnemonic: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d.** Mercury **depresses** because cos 130° is negative — its cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass. Use a **wider tube** to shrink the correction, which is why manometer tubes are specified at 6 mm or more.

questions.stem: The velocity of propagation of water hammer pressure in a pipe carrying water and having diameter 40 cm, pipe thickness 4 mm, with E of the pipe material 2.1 × 10¹¹ Pa and K (bulk modulus of water) 2.1 × 10⁹ Pa, is:
questions.solution:
**1000 m/s** (computed 1024.7 m/s).

For an **elastic** pipe the pressure wave speed accounts for both the compressibility of the water and the stretching of the pipe wall:

> C = √{ 1 / [ ρ ( 1/K + D/(E·e) ) ] }

**Step 1 — the two compliance terms:**
> 1/K = 1/(2.1 × 10⁹) = **4.762 × 10⁻¹⁰**
> D/(E·e) = 0.4/(2.1 × 10¹¹ × 0.004) = 0.4/(8.4 × 10⁸) = **4.762 × 10⁻¹⁰**

The two happen to be **exactly equal** here — the numbers in the question are chosen that way, which is a useful check that you have substituted correctly.

**Step 2 — sum and evaluate:**
> Sum = 9.524 × 10⁻¹⁰
> ρ × Sum = 1000 × 9.524 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 9.524 × 10⁻⁷
> C = √(1/9.524 × 10⁻⁷) = √(1.05 × 10⁶) = **1024.7 m/s ≈ 1000 m/s**

**The physical reading.** For a **perfectly rigid** pipe the D/(Ee) term vanishes and
> C = √(K/ρ) = √(2.1 × 10⁹/1000) = **1449 m/s**

which is the familiar speed of sound in water, and is where option (a) comes from. The elastic pipe gives a **lower** speed — here about 71% of the rigid value — because the wall stretches and absorbs part of the pressure pulse. A thin-walled or flexible pipe reduces the wave speed further, and with it the water-hammer pressure rise.

**Why C matters.** It sets the pipe period **2L/c**, which decides whether a valve closure counts as *sudden* or *gradual*:
- Closure time **< 2L/c** → sudden; Δh = **CV/g**, a very large rise.
- Closure time **> 2L/c** → gradual; Δh = **VL/(gt)**, much smaller — the case worked in Set 1 Q63.

This is exactly why valves on long penstocks are closed slowly and why surge tanks are provided.

examTip.trick: **c = √(K/ρ)** gives 1440 m/s for a rigid pipe, but a real pipe **stretches** too: **c = √(K/ρ)/√(1 + KD/(Et))**. The elasticity of the wall always **reduces** the wave speed below 1440.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rigid 1440, steel 1000–1300, cast iron 1000–1200, PLASTIC only 200–500.** Since **Δp = ρcΔV**, plastic pipe suffers far less water hammer — a genuine practical advantage of PE rising mains over steel.

questions.stem: A rectangular surface 2.5 m × 3 m is immersed vertically in water with its upper edge touching the water surface. Find the depth of the centre of pressure.
questions.solution:
**2 m.**

For a **vertical** plane surface the centre of pressure lies at

> h̄_{cp} = x̄ + I_{G}/(A·x̄)

where x̄ is the depth of the centroid.

**With the upper edge at the free surface and the depth of the plate d = 3 m:**
> x̄ = d/2 = 1.5 m
> A = 2.5 × 3 = 7.5 m²
> I_{G} = bd³/12 = 2.5 × 27/12 = 5.625 m⁴

> h_{cp} = 1.5 + 5.625/(7.5 × 1.5) = 1.5 + 0.5 = **2 m**

**The shortcut.** For any vertical rectangle with its **top edge at the water surface**, the general result collapses to

> h_{cp} = d/2 + d/6 = **2d/3**

so here h_{cp} = 2 × 3/3 = 2 m directly. That **two-thirds of the total depth** result is worth memorising — it is the single most-asked hydrostatics fact.

**Why the centre of pressure sits below the centroid.** Pressure grows linearly with depth, so the lower strips of the plate carry disproportionately more force. The resultant is therefore pulled downward from the centroid. The offset I_{G}/(Ax̄) shrinks as the plate is submerged deeper — at great depth the pressure is nearly uniform over the plate and the centre of pressure approaches the centroid.

The accompanying total force, usually asked in the same question:
> F = γ A x̄ = 9810 × 7.5 × 1.5 = **110.4 kN**

Note the ambiguity in the stem: it gives 2.5 m × 3 m without saying which is vertical. Taking **3 m as the depth** gives 2 m, which matches an option; taking 2.5 m as the depth would give 1.67 m, which does not — so the intended orientation is clear from the choices.

examTip.trick: For a **vertical rectangle with its top edge at the surface**, the centre of pressure is always at **2H/3 from the surface** — that is, **H/3 above the base**. For H = 3 m that is 2 m ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Centroid at H/2, centre of pressure at 2H/3 — ALWAYS below the centroid**, because h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(Ah̄) and the correction is always positive. The deeper the plate is submerged, the more the two converge.

questions.stem: If the total hydroelectric potential of a plant is 84 GW, convert the potential into energy considering a load factor of 60%.
questions.solution:
**441 TWh.**

Energy is power multiplied by time, reduced by the load factor since the plant does not run at full output all year:

> E = P × Load factor × hours in a year

**Substituting:**
> Hours in a year = 24 × 365 = **8760 h**
> E = 84 × 10⁹ W × 0.6 × 8760 h
> E = 4.415 × 10¹⁴ Wh
> E = **441.5 TWh**

**A quick way to see it.** The load factor converts installed capacity into *average* output: 84 GW × 0.6 = **50.4 GW average**. Multiply by 8760 hours and you get 441 504 GWh = 441.5 TWh.

Where the distractors come from, which is instructive:
- **735 TWh** = 84 GW × 8760 h × **1.0** — the answer if you forget the load factor entirely.
- **504 TWh** = mishandling the arithmetic around the 50.4 GW average.

**The engineering point.** Installed capacity and annual energy are different commodities and are sold differently. Capacity is what the plant *can* deliver at an instant; energy is what it actually delivers over the year. The **load factor** (or capacity factor, when measured against installed capacity) links them, and it is what makes a run-of-river scheme in Nepal — high flow in the monsoon, little in the dry season — deliver far less annual energy than its nameplate rating suggests. A storage scheme with the same capacity has a much higher load factor and is correspondingly more valuable.

For context: Nepal's theoretical hydropower potential is about **83 000 MW**, of which roughly **42 000 MW** is considered technically and economically feasible — so the 84 GW in this question is recognisably the theoretical national figure.

examTip.trick: Power × time = energy. **84 GW × 8760 hours = 735 840 GWh = 736 TWh at 100% capacity factor.** The stated 441 TWh implies a capacity factor of about **60%**, which is realistic for hydropower.
examTip.mnemonic: **8760 hours in a year — the number that converts every power figure to an annual energy figure.** And always ask what **capacity factor** is assumed: installed capacity is what the plant *could* do, energy is what it actually delivers.

questions.stem: A column of length L is fixed at both ends. It is equivalent to another column with both ends hinged having length ……
questions.solution:
**L/2.**

Euler's buckling load depends on the **effective length** l_{e}, not the actual length:

> P_{cr} = π²EI / l_{e}²

The effective length is the distance between successive points of contraflexure in the buckled shape — that is, the length of an equivalent **pinned-pinned** column that would buckle at the same load. So the question is simply asking for l_{e}.

For a column **fixed at both ends**, l_{e} = **L/2**, so it behaves exactly like a hinged-hinged column of half the length.

The standard cases, which must be known cold:

| End conditions | Effective length l_{e} | Buckling load |
|---|---|---|
| Both ends hinged (pinned) | **L** | π²EI/L² |
| **Both ends fixed** | **L/2** | **4π²EI/L²** |
| One fixed, one hinged | L/√2 ≈ 0.7L | 2.045π²EI/L² |
| One fixed, one free (cantilever) | **2L** | π²EI/(4L²) |
| Fixed at one end, other fixed in direction but free in position | L | π²EI/L² |

So fixing both ends **quadruples** the buckling load relative to pinned ends, while a cantilever carries only a **quarter** of it — a range of sixteen to one across the table, which is why end restraint is the most powerful lever available to the designer of a compression member.

Note that option (d), L/√2, is the **one-fixed-one-hinged** case, placed here as the near miss.

Two further points that travel with this: buckling depends on **stiffness (E and I), not strength**, so a higher grade of steel does nothing for a slender strut; and in a real frame the effective length is found from the **relative stiffness of the members meeting at each joint**, since ideal fixity is never achieved — IS 800 Annex D and IS 456 Annex E give the charts.

examTip.trick: Equate the effective lengths. **Fixed–fixed: L_e = 0.5L. Hinged–hinged: L_e = L.** So a fixed-fixed column of length L behaves like a hinged column of length **L/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective lengths: hinged–hinged L, fixed–fixed 0.5L, fixed–free 2L, fixed–hinged 0.7L.** Since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, fixing both ends multiplies the buckling load by **four**, and a cantilever column carries only a **quarter**.

questions.stem: If the penetration grade is 62, the penetration value is ……
questions.solution:
**6.2 mm.**

The penetration test measures the **consistency (hardness) of bitumen**. A standard needle under a 100 g load is allowed to penetrate the sample for 5 seconds at 25°C, and the depth reached is reported in **units of one-tenth of a millimetre**.

> Penetration value in mm = **grade / 10**
> So grade 62 → 62 × 0.1 mm = **6.2 mm**

The grade number *is* the penetration in 0.1 mm units, which is the entire content of the question — and the trap is that 62 mm (option a) would be an absurd depth for a needle in bitumen.

**Standard test conditions**, all three of which must be quoted together:
> **25°C, 100 g load, 5 seconds**

**What the grade tells you.** A **higher** penetration means a **softer** bitumen:

| Grade | Character | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| VG-10 / 80-100 | Softer | **Cold climates**, hill roads; stays workable |
| VG-30 / 60-70 | Medium | General road construction — the most used grade |
| VG-40 / 30-40 | Harder | **Hot climates**, heavy traffic, junctions; resists rutting |

The choice is a balance: too soft a grade in a hot climate rutts and bleeds; too hard a grade in a cold climate becomes brittle and cracks. Nepal's range of altitudes means both extremes occur within a single road network, which is why the grade is selected by region.

Indian and Nepali practice has largely moved from penetration grading to **viscosity grading (VG)** under IS 73:2013, because viscosity at 60°C correlates better with in-service performance than a needle test at 25°C. The other consistency tests on the same material are the **softening point** (ring and ball), **ductility** (minimum 40 cm at 27°C) and **viscosity** — and the **Marshall stability** test at 60°C, from Q13 of this paper, tests the compacted mix rather than the binder alone.

examTip.trick: Penetration is measured in **tenths of a millimetre**, so grade 62 means the needle penetrated **6.2 mm**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Penetration grade is in 0.1 mm units** — so a higher number means a SOFTER bitumen. Grades 60/70 and 80/100 are the common paving grades in the region; softer grades are used in colder climates and higher altitudes.

questions.stem: A broad crested weir (C_w = 1.5) having length 30 m and height 2.5 m is placed across a river having RL of upstream bed as 1080 m. If the discharge passing the weir is 90 m³/s, find the RL of the flood wall. (Take freeboard as 1.2 m.)
questions.solution:
**1085.28 m.**

**Step 1 — head over the weir crest.** For a broad crested weir,
> Q = C_{w} · L · H^{3/2}
> 90 = 1.5 × 30 × H^{3/2}
> 90 = 45 H^{3/2}
> H^{3/2} = 2
> H = 2^{2/3} = **1.587 m**

**Step 2 — build up the levels from the river bed.** The flood wall must clear the crest, the head of water flowing over it, and the freeboard:

| Component | Level |
|---|---|
| RL of upstream bed | 1080.000 |
| **+** weir height (crest above bed) | + 2.500 → crest at 1082.500 |
| **+** head over crest, H | + 1.587 → flood level 1084.087 |
| **+** freeboard | + 1.200 |
| **RL of flood wall** | **= 1085.287 ≈ 1085.28 m** |

Why the distractors are placed where they are, which is worth noting as a check on your own working:
- **1084.08 m** — the flood water level itself, if you forget to add the freeboard.
- **1081.58 m** — bed plus H only, omitting the weir height.
- **1083.70 m** — an arithmetic slip in H.

**The engineering point.** The flood wall (or afflux bund) is set above the **afflux level** — the raised upstream water level caused by the obstruction — plus a freeboard for wave action, surge and uncertainty in the design flood. Under-estimating any one of the three components floods the land behind the wall, which is why the build-up is done term by term rather than by a single formula.

Note that H here is the **static head** over the crest; where the approach velocity is significant, the total head H = H_{static} + v²/2g should be used, and C_{w} for a broad crested weir is commonly taken as 1.5 to 1.7 in SI units.

examTip.trick: **Q = C_w L H^(3/2)** for a broad-crested weir. Rearrange for H, then add H to the crest elevation to get the upstream water level.
examTip.mnemonic: **A broad-crested weir forces CRITICAL flow over its crest**, which is exactly why the discharge depends on the head alone and not on downstream conditions. That independence is what makes it a reliable permanent gauging structure — and less sensitive to edge wear than a sharp-crested plate.

questions.stem: How can you strengthen a wall of 50 m length and 5 m height built with brick masonry?
options: By using stronger grade of mortar
questions.solution:
**By constructing buttresses.**

Read the geometry: 50 m long and 5 m high. This is a **long, tall, slender** wall, and its problem is not a shortage of material strength but a shortage of **lateral stability**. It is liable to buckle or overturn under wind, earth pressure or accidental impact, because it has nothing to restrain it out of plane.

A **buttress** — a pier or counterfort projecting from the face at intervals — attacks the actual deficiency. It:
- provides **lateral support**, reducing the effective height or length used in the slenderness calculation;
- greatly increases the **second moment of area** of the wall about the weak axis;
- gives a wider base against **overturning**, since the resisting moment grows with the lever arm.

Why the material options fail. **Stronger brick** (b) and **richer mortar** (c) both raise the *compressive* strength of the masonry, but compressive stress is not what is limiting a 5 m high wall — the axial load in it is modest. Neither does anything for slenderness or out-of-plane stability, so neither addresses the problem. Option (d) is simply false.

**How the code frames it.** IS 1905 designs load-bearing masonry through the **slenderness ratio**:

> SR = effective height / effective thickness  (or effective length / effective thickness)

capped at **27** for load-bearing walls. The permissible compressive stress is then reduced by a **stress reduction factor** that falls as SR rises.
