Buttresses, cross walls, piers and intermediate floors or roof slabs all count as lateral supports and cut the effective height or length, so they pull the slenderness ratio back within limits.

The other measures used for the same purpose: **cross walls** at intervals, **pilasters**, horizontal **RC bands** at plinth, sill, lintel and roof level, and vertical reinforcement at corners — the last two being the core of Nepal's earthquake-resistant masonry detailing in NBC 202 and NBC 203.

examTip.trick: A long, thin, unreinforced masonry wall is vulnerable to **out-of-plane buckling**. Buttresses provide **intermediate lateral support**, reducing the effective height-to-thickness ratio.
examTip.mnemonic: **Buttresses go on the OUTSIDE and work in COMPRESSION; counterforts go on the EARTH side and work in TENSION.** Both stiffen a wall; which you use depends on which face you can occupy.

questions.stem: If part of contract work is assigned to another party, it is called:
questions.solution:
**Sub-contracting.**

The two arrangements differ fundamentally in **who holds the contract with the client**:

| | **Sub-contracting** | **Joint venture (JV)** |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | **Vertical** — main contractor engages a sub-contractor | **Horizontal** — two or more firms combine as equals |
| Contract with client | Held by the **main contractor alone** | Held **jointly** by the JV partners |
| Sub-contractor's link to client | **None** — no privity of contract | — |
| Liability to client | **Main contractor remains fully liable** for the sub-contractor's work | Partners are **jointly and severally liable** |
| Risk and profit | Sub-contractor paid a price; risk largely stays with main contractor | **Shared** among partners per the JV agreement |
| Typical purpose | Specialist trades — piling, electrical, lifts, waterproofing | Meeting large **qualification thresholds**; pooling capacity |

In **sub-contracting**, the main contractor hands over a *portion* of the work — typically a specialist trade it cannot do efficiently itself — while remaining wholly answerable to the client for that work. The client's remedy for defective sub-contract work is against the main contractor, not the sub-contractor.

In a **joint venture**, two or more firms come together as principals to bid and execute jointly, usually because no one of them alone meets the turnover, experience or plant requirements of a large tender.

Option (c) is wrong because these are distinct arrangements, not two names for one thing.

**Points examined alongside, under Nepal's Public Procurement Act 2063:**
- Sub-contracting normally requires the **employer's prior written consent**, and is often capped as a proportion of the contract value.
- The main contractor may not sub-contract the work **in its entirety** — that would be an assignment, which is prohibited.
- **Nominated** sub-contractors are selected by the employer; **domestic** sub-contractors are chosen by the contractor.
- In a JV, one partner is designated **lead partner** and authorised to act for all, and all partners sign the contract and remain jointly and severally liable to the employer.

examTip.trick: Distinguish clearly: **sub-contracting** is assigning part of the work while the main contractor remains responsible to the client; **assignment** transfers the contract itself; **novation** substitutes a new party entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **In sub-contracting the MAIN CONTRACTOR stays liable to the employer** — the sub-contractor has no contract with the client. Most contracts require **written approval** before sub-letting, and prohibit sub-letting the whole works.

questions.stem: What should be the length of weir for a 50 year design flood of 4000 m³/s? Bank to bank width of the river is 280 m.
questions.solution:
**280 m** — the actual bank-to-bank width.

**Step 1 — Lacey's regime waterway.** The stable width a river in alluvium tends to adopt is
> P = 4.75 √Q
> P = 4.75 × √4000 = 4.75 × 63.25 = **300.4 m**

**Step 2 — compare with the river's actual width.**
> Required regime waterway = 300.4 m
> Available bank-to-bank width = **280 m**

Since the regime waterway **exceeds** the width the river actually occupies, the weir cannot be made wider than the channel between the banks. The length of the weir is therefore limited by the site to **280 m**.

**The rule to carry:**

| Condition | Weir length adopted |
|---|---|
| **Lacey's P > bank-to-bank width** | **Bank-to-bank width** |
| Lacey's P < bank-to-bank width | Lacey's P (the river is over-wide; confine it, and provide guide banks) |

So the design length is essentially the **lesser** of the two — you cannot build wider than the valley, and there is no benefit in building wider than the regime width.

**Why it matters.** Building a waterway **narrower** than the regime width causes **afflux** — a raised upstream water level, with increased flooding and a greater tendency to scour, since the same discharge must pass through a smaller section at higher velocity. Building **wider** than the regime width lets the river meander within the structure, causing shoaling, oblique approach flow and attack on one abutment.

Where the waterway is constricted below the regime value, the design must account for the deeper scour that follows: Lacey's regime scour depth is
> R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}

and the anticipated scour is taken as a multiple of R depending on location — deepest at the nose of a guide bank, which is why the **launching apron** of Q34 is sized from it.

examTip.trick: The waterway is set by **Lacey's regime perimeter: P = 4.75√Q**. For Q = 4000: **4.75 × 63.2 = 300 m** — then adjusted for the site.
examTip.mnemonic: **P = 4.75√Q is the regime waterway** — the width a stable alluvial river naturally adopts for that discharge. Constricting a river below its regime width forces deeper **scour**, which is why bridge and barrage waterways are set from this formula rather than from the bank-to-bank width.

questions.stem: Efficiency of chlorine as a disinfectant:
questions.solution:
**Decreases as pH increases.**

When chlorine dissolves in water it hydrolyses to **hypochlorous acid**, which then dissociates:

> Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + H⁺ + Cl⁻
> HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻

The two species are **not** equally effective. Undissociated **HOCl is roughly 80 times more powerful** a disinfectant than the hypochlorite ion OCl⁻, because it is a small, electrically neutral molecule that passes readily through the bacterial cell wall, whereas the negatively charged OCl⁻ is repelled by the negatively charged cell surface.

Raising the pH drives the equilibrium to the **right**, converting potent HOCl into feeble OCl⁻. So disinfection efficiency falls:

| pH | Dominant species |
|---|---|
| 5.5 – 6.5 | **100% HOCl** — most effective |
| 6.6 – 7.4 | HOCl ≫ OCl⁻ |
| **7.5** | **HOCl = OCl⁻** (the pK_a) |
| 7.6 – 9 | OCl⁻ ≫ HOCl |
| > 9 | 100% OCl⁻ — least effective |

Option (c) is the near miss: pH 7 is *good*, but efficiency is higher still at pH 6, so 7 is not the maximum. The relationship is **monotonic decreasing**, not peaked.

**The other factors governing disinfection efficiency**, examined alongside:
- **Contact time** — efficiency rises with time; a minimum of **30 minutes** is required, and the combined effect is expressed as the **C·t** product.
- **Temperature** — higher temperature speeds the kill, so a **lower dose** suffices in warm water; cold water needs more chlorine.
- **Turbidity** — suspended particles shield organisms, which is why water is filtered to below 1 NTU **before** disinfection.
- **Chlorine demand** — ammonia, organic matter, iron and manganese consume chlorine first, as in Q37 of this paper.

Practical consequence: where water is softened or otherwise alkaline, the pH may need to be adjusted **downward before chlorination**, or the dose increased to compensate. Nepal's standard requires a free residual chlorine of **0.1 to 0.2 mg/L** at the consumer's tap.

examTip.trick: Chlorine in water forms **HOCl (hypochlorous acid)**, which is the effective disinfectant, and **OCl⁻ (hypochlorite ion)**, which is far weaker. **Higher pH shifts the balance toward OCl⁻**, so efficiency falls.
examTip.mnemonic: **HOCl is about 80 times more effective than OCl⁻, and low pH favours HOCl.** So chlorinate at **pH below 7.5** where possible. Contact time matters as much as dose — the standard is a **residual of 0.2 mg/l after 30 minutes**.

questions.stem: A barrage with 400 m length is designed across an alluvial river. The U/S and D/S lengths of the proposed guide banks of this barrage will be about:
questions.solution:
**500 m and 100 m.**

Guide bank lengths are expressed as multiples of the barrage waterway length L:

| Arm | Range | Taken here (L = 400 m) |
|---|---|---|
| **Upstream** | **1.0 L to 1.5 L** | 1.25 × 400 = **500 m** |
| **Downstream** | **0.2 L to 0.4 L** | 0.25 × 400 = **100 m** |

So with L = 400 m, taking mid-range multipliers gives **500 m upstream and 100 m downstream** — option (c).

**Why the upstream arm is so much longer.** Upstream, the river has to be gathered in from a wide, meandering flood plain and turned smoothly into a much narrower opening. That approach must be controlled over a long distance, or the flow strikes the structure obliquely and attacks the abutment. Downstream, the flow is already aligned and merely needs to be released and allowed to expand, so a short arm suffices to stop the emerging jet eddying back against the approach embankment.

**Checking the options against the ranges** is the efficient way to answer:
- (a) 400 and 100 → 1.0 L and 0.25 L. Both within range, but 1.0 L is the bare minimum upstream.
- **(c) 500 and 100 → 1.25 L and 0.25 L. Comfortably mid-range on both counts** ✓
- (b) 450 and 150 → 1.125 L and 0.375 L. Also in range, but not the conventional mid-range pick.
- (d) 600 and 200 → 1.5 L and 0.5 L. The downstream value **exceeds** the 0.4 L maximum, so it can be eliminated outright.

Since several options fall inside the permissible bands, the intended answer is the one using the conventional mid-range multipliers of 1.25 L and 0.25 L.

Other details of guide bank design: a **bell mouth** (curved head) upstream of radius about 0.45 L, side slopes of 2H : 1V protected by **stone pitching**, and a **launching apron** at the toe sized from Lacey's scour depth — the subject of Q34 of this paper. Set 1 Q79 asked the same upstream-versus-downstream comparison qualitatively.

examTip.trick: Guide banks (Bell's bunds) are proportioned from the **waterway length L**: upstream arm about **1.0–1.25 L**, downstream about **0.2–0.4 L**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Upstream is much longer than downstream** — the upstream arm must intercept and guide the approaching flow into the opening, which takes distance; the downstream arm only releases it. Their job is to stop a braided river **outflanking** the structure.

questions.stem: What is the consumptive use for a crop in the month of April having a consumptive use coefficient equal to 0.80 and pan evaporation of 35 cm?
questions.solution:
**28.00 cm.**

The consumptive use of a crop is obtained from measured pan evaporation by applying a crop coefficient:

> C_{u} = K_{c} × E_{p}

**Substituting:**
> C_{u} = 0.80 × 35 = **28.00 cm**

Note the direction of the calculation. The coefficient is **less than 1**, so the answer must be **smaller** than the pan evaporation. That single observation eliminates every other option — 43.75 cm is 35/0.8 (dividing instead of multiplying), and 35.80 and 40.80 both exceed the pan figure. Dividing when you should multiply is the classic error here.

**What the quantities mean.**
- **Pan evaporation E_p** is measured directly in a standard **US Class A pan**: 1.21 m in diameter, 25.5 cm deep, water kept 5 to 7.5 cm below the rim.
- **Consumptive use C_u** — also called **evapotranspiration** — is the total water used by the crop: transpiration through the plant plus evaporation from the soil surface.
- The **crop coefficient K_c** converts the reference evaporation into the actual crop demand. It varies with the **crop and, crucially, with its growth stage** — low at sowing when the ground is bare, peaking at full canopy cover, and falling again at maturity.

**Where this sits in the design chain**, which is the reason the question is asked:

> C_{u} → subtract effective rainfall → **NIR** → divide by irrigation efficiency → **GIR** → canal capacity

Set 4 Q42 tested the last step of that chain: the canal is designed for the **gross** irrigation requirement, because it must also carry the conveyance and field application losses.

Other methods of estimating consumptive use, for comparison: **Blaney–Criddle** (temperature and daylight hours), **Penman** and **Penman–Monteith** (energy balance, the FAO reference method), **Hargreaves**, and direct measurement by **lysimeter** or field water balance.

examTip.trick: Consumptive use per day × number of days in the month. April has **30 days** — using 31 is the trap.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the days in the month.** Consumptive use is **ET_crop = K_c × PET**, where K_c varies with the growth stage (about 0.3 at emergence, 1.15 at mid-season). The **crop water requirement** then adds leaching and application losses.

questions.stem: The weight of a pycnometer containing 400 g sand and water full to the top is 2150 g. The weight of the pycnometer full of clean water is 1950 g. If the specific gravity of the soil is 2.5, the water content is:
questions.solution:
**20%.**

The pycnometer method gives water content from four weighings:

> w = [ (W₂ − W₁)/(W₃ − W₄) × (G − 1)/G ] − 1

where W₁ = empty pycnometer, W₂ = pycnometer + moist soil, W₃ = pycnometer + soil + water, W₄ = pycnometer + water only.

**Identifying the given quantities:**
> W₂ − W₁ = mass of moist soil = **400 g**
> W₃ − W₄ = 2150 − 1950 = **200 g**
> G = 2.5

**Substituting:**
> w = [ (400/200) × (2.5 − 1)/2.5 ] − 1
> w = [ 2 × 1.5/2.5 ] − 1
> w = [ 2 × 0.6 ] − 1
> w = 1.2 − 1 = 0.20 = **20%**

**Why the formula works.** The difference W₃ − W₄ is the weight of water *displaced* by the soil solids — the pycnometer is full to the same mark in both weighings, so adding soil pushes out an equal volume of water. That displacement fixes the volume, and hence the weight, of the solids; subtracting the solids from the moist soil leaves the water, and the ratio of the two is the water content.

**Method notes:** the pycnometer is a 900 ml glass jar with a conical brass cap and a 6 mm hole at its apex, so it can be filled to a repeatable mark. The method is quick and suits **sands and gravels**, where oven drying would be slow; it requires the specific gravity G to be known independently, and it is unreliable for clays, from which trapped air is hard to expel.

The **oven-drying** method (IS 2720 Part 2) remains the standard reference: dry at **105–110°C** for 24 hours and take w = (W_wet − W_dry)/W_dry. Field alternatives include the **calcium carbide (rapid moisture meter)** and **sand bath** methods.

Recall from Q51 of this paper the identity **S·e = w·G_s**, which links this water content to the void ratio and degree of saturation.

examTip.trick: The pycnometer works by **displacement**: the difference between the two weighings gives the volume the solids occupy, from which G follows.
examTip.mnemonic: **G for most soils is 2.65–2.75** — quartz sand 2.65, clays slightly higher. A result outside that band means an arithmetic or procedural error, not an exotic soil. Trapped **air bubbles** are the usual culprit, which is why the sample is de-aired before weighing.

questions.stem: If a 2% solution of a sewage sample is incubated for 5 days at 20°C and depletion of oxygen was found to be 5 ppm, the BOD of the sewage is:
questions.solution:
**250 ppm.**

Strong sewage would exhaust all the dissolved oxygen in a BOD bottle long before five days were up, so the sample is **diluted** with aerated distilled water. The measured oxygen depletion is then scaled back up by the dilution factor:

> **BOD = oxygen depletion × dilution factor**
> where DF = 1 / (fractional strength of the solution)

**Step 1 — dilution factor.** A 2% solution means the sample is 2 parts in 100:
> DF = 1/0.02 = **50**

**Step 2 — BOD:**
> BOD = 5 ppm × 50 = **250 ppm**

Equivalently, DF = volume of diluted sample ÷ volume of undiluted sample, so 50 mL of sewage made up to 2500 mL gives the same factor of 50.

**Why dilution is necessary in practice.** Air-saturated water holds only about **9 mg/L** of dissolved oxygen at 20°C. Raw domestic sewage has a BOD₅ of roughly 200 to 300 mg/L — far more than the available oxygen. The dilution is chosen so that the depletion falls in a **reliably measurable band**, conventionally leaving at least 2 mg/L of residual DO and consuming at least 2 mg/L, so the result sits comfortably between the limits of the Winkler titration.

**Conditions of the standard test**, all of which must be stated together: **5 days at 20°C**, in the dark, in a sealed 300 mL bottle. Incubation in the dark prevents algae from *generating* oxygen and confounding the measurement.

By five days about **68%** of the ultimate BOD has been exerted, following
> BOD_{t} = L₀ (1 − 10^{−kt}),  k ≈ 0.1 per day at 20°C

so the ultimate BOD here would be roughly 250/0.68 ≈ 368 ppm. And recall from Q1 of this paper that the **COD of untreated sewage is 1.25 to 1.5 times its BOD**, which would put the COD of this sample somewhere around 310 to 375 ppm.

examTip.trick: **BOD = (DO_initial − DO_final) × dilution factor**, and the dilution factor for a 2% sample is **100/2 = 50**.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOD = DO depletion × dilution factor.** The dilution must be chosen so the DO depletion lands between **2 mg/l and 70% of the initial DO** — too little depletion and the reading is imprecise; too much and the oxygen runs out and the test is invalid.

questions.stem: If the length of a transition curve to be introduced between a straight and a circular curve of radius 500 m is 90 m, the maximum perpendicular offset for the transition curve is:
questions.solution:
**2.70 m.**

For a transition curve of length L introduced between a straight and a circular curve of radius R, the **shift** of the circular curve is

> S = L² / (24R)

and the **maximum perpendicular offset** at the end of the transition is four times that shift:

> Maximum offset = 4S = **L² / (6R)**

**Substituting:**
> S = 90²/(24 × 500) = 8100/12 000 = **0.675 m**
> Maximum offset = 4 × 0.675 = **2.70 m**

Or directly: L²/(6R) = 8100/3000 = 2.70 m ✓

Note how the distractors are built around the same numbers — 0.70 m is close to the shift itself, so confusing the shift with the offset is exactly the error the question is set to catch. Keep the two apart:

| Quantity | Formula | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **Shift** of the circular curve | **L²/(24R)** | 0.675 m |
| **Maximum perpendicular offset** | **L²/(6R) = 4S** | **2.70 m** |

**Why a transition curve is needed at all.** On a straight the radius is infinite and the centrifugal force zero; on a circular curve the radius is R and the force is mv²/R. Introducing that force abruptly would jerk the vehicle sideways. A transition — normally a **clothoid or spiral**, whose radius decreases uniformly with length — lets the centrifugal force build gradually, allows the **superelevation and extra widening to be introduced progressively**, and gives the driver a natural steering path.

The length of transition is taken as the **greatest** of three criteria:
1. **Rate of change of centrifugal acceleration:** L = 0.0215 v³/(CR), with C = 80/(75 + v)
2. **Rate of introduction of superelevation:** L = eN(W + W_e), with N of 1 in 150 for plain and 1 in 60 for hill roads
3. **Empirical (IRC) minimum:** L = 2.7 v²/R for plain and rolling terrain, L = v²/R for mountainous and steep terrain

examTip.trick: The **shift S = L²/(24R)** — the amount by which the circular curve must be moved inward to accommodate the transition.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shift = L²/24R, and the transition is set out so HALF the shift lies on each side.** The transition curve (a spiral/clothoid) exists so that the **radial acceleration builds gradually** rather than jumping from zero to v²/R at a point — which is what makes a sudden curve uncomfortable and unsafe.

questions.stem: In the designation of ordinary Portland cement as OPC 43 grade, the number 43 represents:
questions.solution:
**The 28-day compressive strength in N/mm².**

The grade number of ordinary Portland cement is its **minimum characteristic compressive strength at 28 days**, measured on standard cement–sand mortar cubes (1 : 3 with standard sand, water at 0.4 P + 3%). So OPC 43 must reach at least 43 N/mm² at 28 days.

The three grades and their minimum strengths:

| Grade | 3 days | 7 days | **28 days** | Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OPC 33 | 16 | 22 | **33** | IS 269 |
| **OPC 43** | 23 | 33 | **43** | IS 8112 |
| OPC 53 | 27 | 37 | **53** | IS 12269 |

Note the trap in option (b): the **7-day** strength of OPC 43 happens to be 33 N/mm², which is the *28-day* figure for OPC 33 — an easy confusion, and the reason the grades must be tied to the 28-day age.

**Why 28 days.** Portland cement gains strength rapidly at first and then ever more slowly; by 28 days it has developed roughly 90% of what it will ever reach, and the curve has flattened enough for the value to be a stable basis for specification.

Other properties specified for cement, each with its own test:

| Property | Requirement | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Fineness** | ≥ 225 m²/kg (Blaine) | Air permeability |
| **Initial setting time** | **≥ 30 minutes** | Vicat apparatus |
| **Final setting time** | **≤ 600 minutes (10 h)** | Vicat apparatus |
| **Soundness** | ≤ 10 mm expansion | Le Chatelier |
| Consistency | — | Vicat, for standard consistency P |

Do not confuse the cement grade with the **concrete grade**: M20 concrete is characterised by the 28-day strength of a 150 mm **concrete cube**, whereas OPC 43 refers to a **mortar cube** of cement and standard sand. A higher grade of cement gains strength faster and permits a leaner mix, but it also generates more heat of hydration — a consideration in mass concrete.

examTip.trick: The grade number is the **minimum 28-day compressive strength in N/mm²** of a standard mortar cube — not of concrete, and not the cement's own strength in any other sense.
examTip.mnemonic: **OPC 33, 43 and 53 — the number is the 28-day mortar cube strength.** Higher grades are finer and gain strength faster, which also means **more heat of hydration and more shrinkage** — so OPC 53 is not automatically the better choice for a mass pour.

questions.stem: The main purpose of providing a damp proof course (DPC) in a building is to:
options: Increase the load carrying capacity of the wall
Prevent rising of moisture from the ground into the wall
Provide thermal insulation to the floor
Act as a levelling course for the superstructure
questions.solution:
**To prevent moisture rising from the ground into the wall.**

Soil below a building is almost always damp, and masonry is porous. Water is drawn up through the pores by **capillary action** — the same mechanism as capillary rise in a fine tube, so the finer the pores the higher it climbs. A damp proof course interposes an **impervious barrier** in the path of that rise, normally at **plinth level**, just above ground and below the floor finish.

**Why it matters.** Rising damp produces efflorescence and staining, softens plaster and paint, promotes fungal growth, corrodes any embedded metal, and steadily weakens the mortar. It is far cheaper to exclude the water than to remedy the damage.

**Where DPC is provided:** horizontally at plinth level in all walls; under floors and in basement floors and walls (where it must be continuous and turned up, since it may also resist water *pressure*); at parapets, sills and copings; and vertically where a wall abuts earth.

**Common materials:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete** 1 : 1.5 : 3 or 1 : 2 : 4, **40 to 75 mm** thick, often with a waterproofing admixture | The usual choice at plinth level |
| Bitumen / mastic asphalt | Flexible; good where slight movement is expected |
| Bituminous felt, polythene sheet | Cheap, flexible; must be lapped properly |
| Metal sheet — lead, copper | Durable but expensive |
| Dense engineering brick or stone in cement mortar | Traditional |

The requirements are that the DPC be **impervious, continuous, and free of cracks** — a single break defeats the whole course — and that it not be laid so as to become a **sliding plane** under lateral load, which is why a bond is maintained across it.

Why the other options are wrong: DPC adds nothing to load capacity (option a), gives no useful thermal insulation (c), and although a concrete DPC does incidentally level the plinth, that is a by-product and not its purpose (d).

examTip.trick: A DPC's single job is to **break the capillary path** by which ground moisture climbs into the wall. Anything continuous and impervious works.
examTip.mnemonic: **DPC sits 150 mm above finished ground level and must be CONTINUOUS** — one gap and the damp simply walks around it. It must also be lapped correctly at junctions and never bridged by later rendering or a raised path outside.

questions.stem: As per IS 1200, in measurement of brickwork no deduction is made for an opening whose area is up to:
questions.solution:
**0.1 m².**

IS 1200 (the code of practice for measurement of building works) allows small openings and inserts to be ignored in measuring masonry: **no deduction is made where the area does not exceed 0.1 m²**.

**Why a threshold exists at all.** Cutting brickwork around a small opening costs *more* in labour, not less, and generates waste. The saving in material is trivial and is roughly cancelled by the extra work. Rather than argue over each small hole, the code sets a limit below which the item is simply not deducted — which keeps measurement quick, consistent and free of dispute.

Examples of what falls within the limit: small ventilators, holes for pipes and conduits, ends of beams, posts, purlins and rafters bearing in the wall, and wall plates up to 0.1 m² in section.

The measurement conventions that accompany this:

| Item | Convention |
|---|---|
| Brickwork | Measured in **m³**; no deduction ≤ 0.1 m² |
| Openings for doors and windows | Deducted at the **size of the frame opening** |
| Plaster | Measured in **m²**; no deduction ≤ 0.5 m². For openings up to 3 m², deduction on **one face only** |
| Reinforcement | Measured by **weight**, laps and hooks included; no deduction for the volume it occupies in concrete |
| Excavation | Measured in **m³**; no deduction for the volume of the footing |

Note the different threshold for **plaster** (0.5 m²) — mixing the two figures up is the usual error, and it is why the plaster row is worth learning alongside this one.

The purpose of all these rules is that a bill of quantities prepared by one engineer and priced by another should describe **the same work**. Measurement conventions are as much a part of estimating as the arithmetic, and disputes on site far more often turn on how something was measured than on the rate applied to it.

examTip.trick: The rule exists because measuring and deducting a tiny opening costs more in surveyor's time than the brickwork is worth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brickwork: no deduction below 0.1 m². Plastering: no deduction below 0.5 m².** Two different thresholds in the same code — check which trade the question is about, because the numbers are deliberately different.

questions.stem: In a flow net, the flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at:
questions.solution:
**90°.**

A flow net is the graphical solution of Laplace's equation for two-dimensional seepage,

> ∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂z² = 0

and its two families of curves are **mathematically orthogonal**. The reason is physical: water flows in the direction of the steepest hydraulic gradient, which is **normal** to a line of constant head. So a flow line must cross an equipotential line at a right angle everywhere.

The properties of a correctly drawn flow net — a standard list:

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| Flow lines and equipotentials meet at **90°** | Orthogonality |
| The figures formed are **curvilinear squares** | Length ≈ breadth in each field |
| **Equal quantity of flow** passes between adjacent flow lines | Each flow channel carries Δq |
| **Equal head drop** between adjacent equipotentials | Each drop is H/N_d |
| Flow lines never intersect one another | — |
| Boundaries are themselves flow lines or equipotentials | Impervious boundary = flow line; permeable surface = equipotential |

**What the net is used for.** Once drawn, it yields the three quantities the engineer needs:

> **Seepage discharge:** q = k · H · (N_f / N_d)
> **Pore pressure** at any point, from the number of drops passed
> **Exit gradient:** i_{E} = (H/N_d)/Δl at the downstream exit — the quantity that governs **piping**

where N_f is the number of flow channels, N_d the number of equipotential drops, H the total head loss and k the coefficient of permeability.

The exit gradient is the critical output, because piping begins when it approaches the **critical hydraulic gradient** i_{cr} = (G_s − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1 — the condition examined in Set 1 Q3. A flow net therefore turns a qualitative worry about seepage into a number that can be compared against a factor of safety of 4 to 5.

In **anisotropic** soil, where k_x ≠ k_z, the section is first transformed by scaling one coordinate by √(k_z/k_x); the net is drawn orthogonal in the transformed section, and the equivalent permeability is √(k_x k_z).

examTip.trick: Velocity is **tangential** to a flow line and **normal** to an equipotential, so the two families must cross at right angles. The **square mesh** is the check that the net is drawn correctly.
examTip.mnemonic: **q = kH(N_f/N_d), and COUNT THE SPACES, NOT THE LINES.** The net's safety-critical output is the **exit gradient** in the smallest downstream field, checked against i_c ≈ 1 with a factor of **4 to 7**.

questions.stem: For obtaining undisturbed soil samples, the area ratio of the sampler should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**10%.**

The **area ratio** measures how much soil the sampling tube has to displace as it is pushed in:

> A_{r} = (D₂² − D₁²)/D₁² × 100%

where D₁ is the **inside** diameter of the cutting edge and D₂ the **outside** diameter.

The displaced soil must go somewhere — it is forced sideways and compresses the surrounding ground, and some of it drags into the tube along the walls. The larger the area ratio, the more the sample is remoulded and the less it represents the soil in place. Keeping **A_r ≤ 10%** limits that disturbance enough for the sample to be treated as undisturbed for strength and consolidation testing.

The two contrasting samplers make the point:

| Sampler | Area ratio | Sample |
|---|---|---|
| **Thin-walled Shelby tube** | **≈ 10%** | **Undisturbed** — for c_u, consolidation |
| **Split-spoon (SPT sampler)** | **≈ 110%** | **Disturbed** — for classification and index tests only |

That is why the standard penetration test yields an **N-value and a disturbed sample**, and never a specimen fit for a triaxial test.

The companion design ratios for a sampling tube:

| Ratio | Formula | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Area ratio** | (D₂² − D₁²)/D₁² | **≤ 10%** (≤ 20% acceptable for stiff soils) |
| **Inside clearance** | (D₃ − D₁)/D₁ | **0.5 to 3%** — lets the sample expand slightly so it does not jam or stick |
| **Outside clearance** | (D₂ − D₄)/D₄ | **0 to 2%** — reduces skin friction on withdrawal |

where D₃ is the inside diameter of the tube above the cutting edge and D₄ the outside diameter of the cutting edge.

Other requirements for genuinely undisturbed sampling: a **recovery ratio** near 1.0, a sharp cutting edge, steady rather than hammered penetration, immediate **sealing with wax** to preserve the moisture content, and careful transport — a sample disturbed in the vehicle is as useless as one disturbed in the ground.

examTip.trick: **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100.** Keeping it under 10% limits the soil the sampler wall has to displace, and hence the disturbance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under 10% for undisturbed sampling.** A thick-walled **split spoon is around 100%** — which is precisely why an SPT sample is a **disturbed** sample and can never be used for a strength or consolidation test.

questions.stem: A floating body is in stable equilibrium when the metacentre lies:
questions.solution:
**Above the centre of gravity.**

When a floating body tilts through a small angle, the submerged shape changes and the **centre of buoyancy B** shifts sideways. The **metacentre M** is the point where the new line of buoyant force crosses the original centreline.

The stability then follows from where M sits relative to the centre of gravity G:

| Position of M | GM | Moment created | Equilibrium |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Above G** | **Positive** | **Righting** — restores the body | **Stable** |
| Below G | Negative | Overturning — tilts it further | **Unstable** |
| Coincident with G | Zero | None | Neutral |

With **M above G**, the buoyant force acting up through the shifted B and the weight acting down through G form a couple that pushes the body **back** towards upright. If M falls below G the same couple acts the other way and the body capsizes.

**Computing the metacentric height:**

> **GM = I/V − BG**

where I is the second moment of area of the water-plane section about the axis of tilt and V the displaced volume. So a **wide** vessel has a large I and is stiff; a narrow one is tender.

The experimental determination, worth knowing:
> GM = (w · x) / (W · tan θ)

moving a known weight w a distance x across the deck and measuring the resulting tilt θ.

**A design tension the examination likes.** A **large** GM gives strong stability but a short, violent rolling period — uncomfortable and hard on the structure. A **small** positive GM gives an easy roll but little margin. The period of roll is
> T = 2π √(k²/(g · GM))

so GM is chosen as a compromise, not simply maximised.

Note the contrast with a **fully submerged** body, where the shape does not change on tilting: there the metacentre concept does not apply, and stability requires simply that **B lie above G**.

examTip.trap: Applying the **submerged**-body rule (B above G) to a **floating** body is the standard error — almost every ship has B **below** G and is perfectly stable.
examTip.trick: For a floating body **B MOVES** as it heels, because the shape of the displaced volume changes. That is what creates the metacentre and what makes stability possible with B below G.
examTip.mnemonic: **GM = BM − BG with BM = I/V, and I ∝ beam³** — which is why a raft is very stable and a log rolls. **Submerged bodies** are the different case: B is fixed, BM = 0, so B really must be above G.

questions.stem: A unit hydrograph is the direct runoff hydrograph resulting from an effective rainfall of:
questions.solution:
**1 cm of effective rainfall, uniformly distributed over the catchment**, occurring at a uniform rate within a specified duration.

The full definition has three parts, and all three must be stated:
1. The **depth** of effective (net) rainfall is **1 cm**.
2. It is distributed **uniformly** over the whole catchment.
3. It falls at a uniform rate within a **specified duration** — which is why we speak of a *2-hour* or *6-hour* unit hydrograph, never simply "the" unit hydrograph of a catchment.

Note that **effective rainfall** means the portion that becomes direct runoff — total rainfall less infiltration, interception and depression storage. So a unit hydrograph relates 1 cm of *runoff*, not 1 cm of rain.

**The assumptions on which it rests:**

| Assumption | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Linearity / proportionality** | 2 cm of effective rainfall produces ordinates **twice** those of the unit hydrograph |
| **Superposition** | Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks can be added, offset in time |
| **Time invariance** | The catchment's response does not change from storm to storm |

Those three properties are what make it useful: from one unit hydrograph, the flood from any storm pattern can be synthesised by scaling and adding.

**A property worth remembering:** the **area under a unit hydrograph** always equals 1 cm of runoff over the catchment area, whatever the duration. That is the standard check on a derived unit hydrograph — if the volume does not come to A × 1 cm, the baseflow separation or the rainfall excess is wrong.

**Limitations.** It assumes uniform rainfall over the whole catchment, so it is unsuitable for catchments larger than about **5000 km²**, and it cannot represent snowmelt or highly non-uniform storms.

Where no gauged record exists — the common situation in Nepal — a **synthetic unit hydrograph** is derived from catchment characteristics by Snyder's method or the SCS dimensionless hydrograph, or the regional methods of Q17 of this paper are used instead.

examTip.trap: Two errors hide here: the depth is **EFFECTIVE** rainfall (after losses), not total; and the duration names the **rainfall**, not the length of the hydrograph.
examTip.trick: Unit means **1 cm**, distributed **uniformly** in space and at a constant rate through the stated duration — and the result is a **DIRECT runoff** hydrograph, with base flow excluded.
examTip.mnemonic: **Proportionality and superposition.** Doubling the rainfall doubles every ordinate but leaves the **time base unchanged** — a direct consequence of assuming linearity, which real catchments only approximate.

questions.stem: The relationship between the modulus of elasticity E, the modulus of rigidity G and Poisson's ratio μ is:
questions.solution:
**E = 2G(1 + μ).**

An isotropic elastic material has only **two independent** elastic constants; the others follow. The two standard relations are

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)**  — links E to the shear modulus
> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** — links E to the bulk modulus

and eliminating μ between them gives
> E = 9KG/(3K + G)

Option (c) is the trap: **3K(1 − 2μ)** is the *bulk* modulus relation, offered here with G substituted for K.

**Typical values for steel** make the relation easy to check:
> μ = 0.3, G = 80 GPa
> E = 2 × 80 × 1.3 = **208 GPa** ✓ — close to the accepted 200–210 GPa

**Useful special cases:**

| μ | Relation | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | E = 2G | No lateral contraction (cork is near this) |
| **0.25** | **E = 2.5G** | Convenient exam value; also K = E/1.5 |
| 0.3 | E = 2.6G | **Steel** |
| 0.5 | E = 3G, **K → ∞** | **Incompressible** — rubber; the theoretical upper limit |

The limits on μ are worth knowing: from **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**, requiring K to stay positive forces **μ < 0.5**, and for ordinary materials **0 ≤ μ ≤ 0.5**. Concrete sits near 0.15 to 0.20, steel at 0.3.

**Definitions, for completeness:**
- **E** — normal stress ÷ normal strain, from an axial tension test.
- **G** — shear stress ÷ shear strain, from a torsion test.
- **K** — hydrostatic pressure ÷ volumetric strain.
- **μ** — lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain, taken as a positive number.

The practical value of the relation is that a single tension test gives E, and one further constant then fixes the whole elastic behaviour — which is why torsion of a shaft (Set 1 Q90) can be predicted from tensile data.

examTip.trap: **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** is offered and is a genuine relation — but for the **BULK** modulus. Correct in form, wrong constant.
examTip.trick: Sanity-check at the limits: μ = 0.5 gives E = 3G, and K → ∞ (incompressible) ✓. Any relation that misbehaves there is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **G ≈ 0.4E and K ≈ 0.83E for steel (μ = 0.3).** Only **two** elastic constants are independent for an isotropic material — every other one follows.

questions.stem: The degree of static indeterminacy of a beam fixed at both ends (a plane structure) is:
questions.solution:
**3.**

Static indeterminacy is the excess of unknown reactions over available equilibrium equations:

> D_{s} = (number of unknown reactions) − (number of equilibrium equations)

**For a plane fixed-fixed beam:**
> Each fixed support provides **3** restraints — horizontal force, vertical force and moment.
> Total unknowns = 3 + 3 = **6**
> Plane equilibrium equations = **3** (ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0)
> D_{s} = 6 − 3 = **3**

Option (d), 6, is the count of *reactions*, not the indeterminacy — the commonest slip here.

The standard beams, worth knowing as a set:

| Beam | Reactions | D_s |
|---|---|---|
| Simply supported (pin + roller) | 3 | **0** — determinate |
| Cantilever | 3 | **0** — determinate |
| **Propped cantilever** | 4 | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | **6** | **3** |
| Continuous over 3 supports (pin + 2 rollers) | 4 | 1 |

**Why it matters.** The degree of indeterminacy is the number of **compatibility conditions** — statements about deflection or rotation — that must be added to statics before the structure can be solved. A propped cantilever needs one (Set 1 Q23 used exactly that), a two-hinged arch needs one (Q28 of this paper), and a fixed beam needs three.

Methods for solving them: consistent deformation, the **three-moment equation**, **slope-deflection**, **moment distribution**, and matrix stiffness analysis.

For general plane frames the formula is
> **D_s = 3m + r − 3j**

with m members, r support reactions and j joints; for plane trusses it is D_s = m + r − 2j. Total indeterminacy is D_s plus the **kinematic** indeterminacy (the number of unknown joint displacements), which is what the stiffness method works with instead.

A practical note: indeterminate structures are **stiffer and safer** — they have alternative load paths, so the loss of one member need not cause collapse — but they develop stresses from **settlement, temperature change and shrinkage**, which a determinate structure simply accommodates by moving.

examTip.trick: **D_s = r − 3** for a plane beam with no internal hinges. A fixed end has **three** reaction components (H, V, M), so two fixed ends give **6 − 3 = 3**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixed both ends 3, propped cantilever 1, simply supported 0.** Each internal **hinge** subtracts one. Caution: the count checks **degree, not stability** — three parallel or three concurrent reactions give a valid count and an unstable structure.

questions.stem: The development length L_d of a reinforcing bar of diameter φ is given by:
questions.solution:
**L_d = φσ_s / (4τ_bd).**

**Derivation** — it is worth deriving rather than memorising, because the derivation makes the 4 obvious. Development length is the embedment needed for **bond** to transfer the full bar force into the concrete. Equate the two:

> Force in the bar = (πφ²/4) × σ_s
> Bond resistance = (surface area) × τ_bd = (πφ L_d) × τ_bd

Setting them equal:
> (πφ²/4)σ_s = πφ L_d τ_bd
> **L_d = φσ_s/(4τ_bd)** ✓

The 4 comes from the ratio of the bar's **cross-sectional area to its perimeter** — which is why it cannot be anything else.

**The terms:**
- σ_s is the stress in the bar at ultimate, taken as **0.87 f_y**.
- τ_bd is the **design bond stress**, from IS 456 cl. 26.2.1.1: **1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7 and 1.9 N/mm²** for M20, M25, M30, M35 and M40 respectively. For **deformed bars** this is increased by **60%**, and for bars in **compression** by a further 25%.

**Worked value — Fe 415 in M20, deformed:**
> τ_bd = 1.2 × 1.6 = 1.92 N/mm²
> L_d = φ × 0.87 × 415/(4 × 1.92) = **47φ**

which is the familiar rule of thumb that development length is roughly **47 diameters** for Fe 415 in M20, and about **56φ** for Fe 500 in M20. Higher concrete grades shorten it; higher steel grades lengthen it.

**Why it matters.** If a bar is not developed, it pulls out of the concrete and the member fails at a load far below its flexural capacity — a **bond failure**, brittle and sudden. Development length therefore governs where bars may be curtailed or lapped, the anchorage required into supports, and the size of the bend and hook at a bar end. IS 456 permits a **standard bend or hook** to count towards the anchorage: a 90° bend is worth 8φ and a standard U-hook 16φ, which is how the full L_d is achieved in a shallow support.

Related: **lap length** in tension is taken as the greater of L_d or 30φ, and laps should be staggered and kept away from sections of maximum moment.

examTip.trick: Derive it from equilibrium: the bar's **tensile force** (πφ²/4)σ_s must be resisted by the **bond force** on its surface, πφL_d τ_bd. Equating gives **L_d = φσ_s/(4τ_bd)** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Force in the bar equals bond around its surface — that is the whole derivation.** Two adjustments: **τ_bd is increased 60% for deformed bars** and a further 25% for compression. Insufficient development length is a real and common detailing failure, especially at supports and laps.

questions.stem: In a post-tensioned member prestressed with a single cable, which loss of prestress does not occur?
options: Loss due to creep of concrete
Loss due to relaxation of steel
Loss due to elastic shortening of concrete
Loss due to shrinkage of concrete
questions.solution:
**Loss due to elastic shortening of concrete.**

The reason is one of sequence. In **post-tensioning**, the concrete is cast and hardened first, and the cable is stressed **against the hardened member**. The elastic shortening of the concrete therefore happens *while* the jack is still applying and measuring the force — so the jack simply takes up that movement, and with a **single** cable there is no loss on that account at all.

In **pre-tensioning**, the wire is stretched first and the concrete cast around it. When the wire is released, the concrete shortens elastically and drags the steel with it, and the prestress falls immediately. Elastic shortening is therefore always a loss in pre-tensioning.

**The important qualification:** with **several cables** stressed in sequence, tensioning the second cable shortens the concrete again and so relaxes the first. Each cable except the last suffers some elastic-shortening loss. The loss is nil only for a **single** cable — which is exactly what the question specifies.

The complete list of losses:

| Loss | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|
| **Elastic shortening** | **Yes** | **No** (single cable); partial for multiple cables |
| Creep of concrete | Yes | Yes |
| Shrinkage of concrete | Yes (larger — concrete is younger) | Yes (smaller) |
| Relaxation of steel | Yes | Yes |
| **Friction / wobble in duct** | **No** | **Yes** — a major loss in long or curved cables |
| **Anchorage slip (draw-in)** | No | **Yes** |

Total losses per IS 1343 are taken as roughly **20% for pre-tensioned** and **15% for post-tensioned** members. The two losses unique to post-tensioning — **friction** and **anchorage slip** — are the price paid for avoiding elastic shortening, which is why post-tensioning is not simply the better option.

Losses divide into **immediate** (elastic shortening, anchorage slip, friction) and **time-dependent** (creep, shrinkage, relaxation). The time-dependent group is why prestressed members need high-strength concrete of grade M30 or above, and low-relaxation strand.

examTip.trap: Elastic shortening loss is the trap for a **single** tendon: with only one cable, it is tensioned **against the already-shortened concrete**, so there is **no elastic shortening loss at all**.
examTip.trick: Separate the loss lists. **Pre-tensioning:** elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage, relaxation. **Post-tensioning:** friction, anchorage slip, creep, shrinkage, relaxation — and elastic shortening **only if there are multiple tendons stressed sequentially**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Friction and anchorage slip belong to POST-tensioning; elastic shortening (single tendon) does not.** Total losses typically 15–20% pre-tensioned, 20–25% post-tensioned.

questions.stem: The effective throat thickness of a fillet weld between two plates meeting at right angles is:
questions.solution:
**0.7 × the size of the weld.**

A fillet weld between plates at 90° has a triangular cross-section whose two legs are the **size** s. Its weakest plane is the one across the **throat** — the shortest distance from the root to the hypotenuse — and for a right-angled isosceles triangle that distance is

> t_{e} = s / √2 = **0.707 s ≈ 0.7 s**

So IS 800 takes the effective throat thickness as **K × s**, where K depends on the angle between the fusion faces:

| Angle between fusion faces | **K** |
|---|---|
| **60° – 90°** | **0.70** |
| 91° – 100° | 0.65 |
| 101° – 106° | 0.60 |
| 107° – 113° | 0.55 |
| 114° – 120° | 0.50 |

The strength of the weld then follows:

> Design strength per unit length = **t_{e} × f_{u} / (√3 γ_{mw})**

with f_u the smaller ultimate tensile strength of the parts joined, and γ_{mw} = 1.25 for shop welding and 1.5 for site welding — site welds are derated because the quality is harder to control.

**Other rules for fillet welds** that accompany this:
- **Effective length** = actual length − 2s, allowing for the incomplete throat at the two ends; it must be at least **4s**.
- **Minimum size** depends on the thicker plate: 3 mm for plates up to 10 mm, rising to 8 mm for plates over 32 mm — to avoid rapid cooling and cracking.
- **Maximum size** along the edge of a plate is limited to **thickness − 1.5 mm**, so the plate edge is not melted away.
- **End returns** of twice the weld size are provided at the ends to protect against tearing.
- **Intermittent** welds must have a length of at least 4s or 40 mm.

Note the contrast with a **butt weld**, where the effective throat is taken as the **full thickness** of the thinner plate for a complete-penetration weld — so a butt weld develops the full strength of the member, while a fillet weld never does. That is why butt welds are used for main tension members and fillet welds for connections and brackets.

examTip.trick: The **throat** is the shortest dimension across the weld's triangular section: **t = 0.707 × size**, since cos 45° = 0.707 for the usual 90° fillet.
examTip.mnemonic: **Throat = 0.7 × size, and strength is calculated on the THROAT, never on the leg length.** Also remember the minimum size depends on the **thicker** plate (to avoid rapid cooling and cracking) while the maximum depends on the **thinner** one.

questions.stem: The self-cleansing velocity in a sanitary sewer is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**0.6 m/s** — commonly specified as 0.6 to 0.9 m/s at minimum flow.

Sewage carries grit, silt and organic solids. If the velocity falls too low these settle out, and the deposit reduces the section, causes blockage, and decomposes anaerobically to generate **hydrogen sulphide** — which is both toxic and, once oxidised to sulphuric acid on the crown of the pipe, destructive to concrete. The **self-cleansing velocity** is the minimum velocity that keeps the solids in suspension so the sewer scours itself.

The design must satisfy limits at **both** ends of the flow range:

| Condition | Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum velocity** (at minimum flow) | **0.6 – 0.9 m/s** | Self-cleansing; prevents deposition and H₂S |
| **Maximum velocity** (at peak flow) | **2.4 – 3.0 m/s** | Prevents **erosion** of the pipe invert |

The sewer must therefore be sized so that it is self-cleansing when flows are low **and** non-scouring when they are high — which is the essential difficulty in sewer design, since sanitary flows vary widely through the day and grow over the design period.

**The design velocity is computed by Manning's equation**, and the classic solution to the low-flow problem is a **circular section flowing part-full**: because the hydraulic radius of a circular pipe at partial depth is close to that at full depth, the velocity holds up well as the depth falls. Sewers are conventionally designed to run about **half to three-quarters full** at the design peak, leaving capacity for growth and for ventilation.

Related figures worth carrying: velocity is **maximum at 0.81D** depth and **discharge maximum at 0.95D** — so a pipe actually carries slightly more flow just before it runs full than when full. For **storm** sewers the minimum velocity is taken a little higher, around 0.75 to 0.9 m/s, because they carry heavier grit.

Where the ground is flat and gravity cannot deliver the minimum velocity, the remedies are a **flushing tank**, a steeper local gradient, or a **pumping station** to lift the sewage and restart the gradient.

examTip.trick: The velocity must be high enough to keep solids in suspension so the sewer does not silt and block.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum 0.6–0.75 m/s at the MINIMUM daily flow; maximum 3 m/s to avoid eroding the invert.** The binding condition is the minimum-flow one, and it is what makes sewer design harder than water main design — a new development's early flows are a small fraction of the ultimate design flow.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower plant:
options: Large storage is provided to regulate seasonal flow
The plant operates only during the dry season
Water is pumped back to the upper reservoir during off-peak hours
Little or no storage is provided, so output follows the river flow
questions.solution:
**Little or no storage is provided, so output follows the natural river flow.**

A run-of-river scheme diverts water from the river through a headworks, carries it along a headrace to a forebay, and drops it through a penstock to the powerhouse, returning it to the river downstream. There is no large reservoir, so **generation at any moment is limited by whatever the river happens to be carrying**.

The consequence in Nepal is stark and is what makes this worth knowing: monsoon flows are many times the dry-season flows, so a run-of-river plant generates near capacity from roughly June to September and only a fraction of it in the winter and spring months. Its **firm power** — the output available reliably, read off the flow duration curve at Q₉₀ or Q₉₅ — may be only 20 to 30% of installed capacity.

The plant types compared:

| Type | Storage | Output | Duty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Run-of-river** | **None or pondage only** | **Follows river flow** | Base load, seasonal |
| Storage (reservoir) | **Large — seasonal regulation** | Controlled at will | Base and peak |
| **Pumped storage** | Two reservoirs | Net consumer of energy; shifts it in time | **Peak load** |
| Run-of-river with **pondage** | Small — hours to a day | Daily peaking within the day's flow | Daily peaking |

So option (a) describes a **storage** scheme and option (c) a **pumped storage** scheme.

**Why run-of-river dominates in Nepal.** The steep terrain gives high head over short distances, so large power is available without a big dam; and the environmental, resettlement and sediment problems of a large reservoir in the Himalaya are severe. Most Nepali projects — Khimti, Bhotekoshi, Upper Tamakoshi — are run-of-river or run-of-river with pondage.

The cost of that choice is the **seasonal deficit**, which is why storage projects and regional interconnection matter for dry-season supply, and why **pondage** (a small forebay giving a few hours of regulation) is added wherever possible so the plant can at least follow the daily demand peak.

examTip.trick: Run-of-river means **no significant reservoir**, so the plant can only use the flow the river happens to be providing at that moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Output follows the hydrograph — high in monsoon, low in the dry season.** That is exactly Nepal's problem: peak demand in winter, peak flow in summer. The design flow is usually taken from the **flow duration curve at about Q₄₀**, and a **peaking pondage** can shift a few hours of output into the evening peak.

questions.stem: The downstream profile of an ogee spillway is shaped to:
options: Follow the lower nappe of a freely falling jet
Increase the discharge coefficient beyond unity
Create a hydraulic jump on the spillway face
Reduce the height of the dam
questions.solution:
**To follow the shape of the lower nappe of a freely falling jet**, so the flow stays in contact with the spillway surface.

An **ogee (overflow) spillway** takes an S-shaped profile that reproduces the underside of the nappe that water would form if it fell freely over a sharp-crested weir at the design head.

**Why that shape.** If the profile were flatter than the nappe, the sheet of water would ride clear of the surface, leaving a gap in which the pressure falls below atmospheric. That negative pressure invites **cavitation** — vapour bubbles forming and collapsing violently against the concrete, pitting and eventually destroying it — and it makes the nappe unstable, so it slaps against the surface. If the profile were steeper, the water would press on the surface and positive pressure would reduce the discharge.

Matching the nappe exactly gives **atmospheric pressure along the whole surface at the design head**, which is the optimum: no cavitation risk, and the maximum discharge for the head available.

The profile is defined by
> x^{n} = K H_{d}^{n−1} y

with K and n depending on the upstream face slope (K = 2.0, n = 1.85 for a vertical upstream face), and H_d the design head.

**Behaviour away from the design head**, which is the examinable consequence:

| Head | Pressure on the crest | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **H = H_d** | Atmospheric | Optimum; C_d ≈ 2.2 (SI) |
| H < H_d | **Positive** | Nappe presses on surface; discharge slightly reduced |
| **H > H_d** | **Negative (sub-atmospheric)** | **Cavitation risk**; discharge slightly increased |

So the design head is usually chosen a little **below** the maximum expected head, accepting mild negative pressure at extreme floods rather than positive pressure through the whole normal range.

Why the other options fail: a discharge coefficient greater than unity (b) is not a meaningful goal, since C_d is dimensional here; a hydraulic jump (c) is deliberately confined to the **stilling basin at the toe**, never on the face, where high velocity flow must stay smooth; and the profile has no bearing on dam height (d).

The energy is dissipated **at the toe**, by a stilling basin, roller bucket or ski jump according to the tail water depth — the choice examined in Set 1 Q44.

The flow remains in contact with the surface.

examTip.trick: The **ogee** profile is shaped to match the **underside of a freely falling nappe** at the design head, so the sheet of water just stays in contact with the crest and the pressure on it is close to atmospheric.
examTip.mnemonic: **At LOWER heads the water presses on the crest (safe); at HIGHER heads it tends to lift off, creating sub-atmospheric pressure and CAVITATION risk.** That asymmetry is why the design head is chosen carefully and why crest profiles are built to tight tolerances.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of a settling basin in the headworks of a hydropower plant is to:
options: Store water for peak load generation
Dissipate the energy of the incoming flow
Remove suspended sediment before water enters the headrace and turbine
Measure the discharge diverted from the river
questions.solution:
**To remove suspended sediment before the water reaches the headrace and the turbine.**

Himalayan rivers carry very high sediment loads, and much of that sediment is **quartz and feldspar** — minerals harder than the steel of a turbine runner. Passed through the machine at high velocity, it acts as an abrasive: it erodes buckets and guide vanes, destroys the profile the runner was designed to, and drives efficiency down. Repair means dismantling the unit, so the plant loses generation as well as incurring the cost.

A settling basin is therefore placed immediately after the intake. It works on the simplest of principles: **widen the section so the velocity falls**, and give the water enough residence time for particles above a target size to settle out.

> Basin length ≈ (depth × flow velocity) / (settling velocity of the design particle)

with the settling velocity from **Stokes' law** for fine particles.

**Design targets:**
- Flow velocity reduced to about **0.2 to 0.4 m/s**.
- Particles above about **0.2 mm** removed for a Francis turbine, and down to **0.1 mm** or finer for a high-head Pelton, since abrasion damage rises steeply with head.
- Provision for **flushing** the accumulated deposit back to the river, either intermittently through gates or continuously in a hopper-bottomed basin.

Why the other options are wrong: **storage for peaking** is the job of a forebay or pondage (option a); **energy dissipation** belongs to the structures at a spillway toe (b); and **discharge measurement** is done by a weir, flume or gauge (d).

The sediment defences work in sequence, and it is worth seeing them as a set: a **trash rack** at the intake stops floating debris; a **gravel trap** takes out the coarse bed load; the **settling basin** removes the finer suspended fraction; and on an irrigation headworks a **silt excluder** — the subject of Q33 of this paper — keeps the bottom, silt-laden layer out of the canal in the first place. Prevention at the intake is always cheaper than extraction downstream.

examTip.trick: A settling (desilting) basin **slows the water so suspended sediment falls out** before it reaches the turbine — where suspended sand acts as an abrasive.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan rivers carry very heavy sediment, and quartz sand ERODES turbine runners fast** — Pelton needles and Francis runners can lose their profile in a single monsoon. The basin is sized so the settling velocity of the target particle (often 0.2 mm) is achieved within the basin length.

questions.stem: In a cement concrete (rigid) pavement, expansion joints are provided primarily to:
options: Allow the slab to expand with rise in temperature
Allow the slab to contract during setting
Provide drainage of the pavement surface
questions.solution:
**To allow the slab to expand as the temperature rises.**

Concrete expands when heated. A long slab restrained from expanding develops very large **compressive stresses**, which cause it to buckle upward — "blow-up" — at a joint or crack. An **expansion joint** is a full-depth gap, typically 20 to 25 mm wide, filled with a compressible filler and sealed at the top, that gives the slab somewhere to grow into.

The joints in a rigid pavement, each with a distinct purpose, which is exactly what this question tests:

| Joint | Purpose | Typical spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **Expansion** | **Accommodate expansion in hot weather** | 50 – 140 m |
| **Contraction** | Relieve **shrinkage and contraction** stresses; control where cracks form | 4.5 m (plain), longer with reinforcement |
| **Warping (hinge)** | Relieve **curling** stresses from the temperature gradient through the slab depth | Along the longitudinal centreline |
| **Construction** | Where the day's paving stops | As required |

So option (b) describes a **contraction** joint and option (c) describes the function of **dowel bars**, not of the joint itself.

**Load transfer** is provided *across* joints by **dowel bars** — plain round bars, half bonded and half free to slide, so the slabs can move relative to one another while shear is still carried across the joint. **Tie bars**, by contrast, are deformed and fully bonded, and are used at longitudinal joints to hold slabs together rather than to transfer load.

**The two stress systems in a rigid pavement**, which explain why so many joints are needed:
- **Uniform temperature change** → expansion and contraction along the slab → handled by expansion and contraction joints.
- **Temperature gradient** through the depth (hot top, cool bottom by day; reversed at night) → the slab tries to curl and its own weight restrains it → **warping stresses**, handled by warping joints.

This is the essential difference from a flexible pavement, which simply deforms and needs no joints at all. Rigid pavement design (IRC 58, Westergaard analysis) therefore combines **load stresses** with these **temperature stresses**, and the critical combination governs the slab thickness.

examTip.trick: Rigid pavement joints each solve a different problem: **expansion** joints allow growth in heat, **contraction** joints control shrinkage cracking, **warping** joints relieve temperature curling, and **construction** joints mark a day's work.
examTip.mnemonic: **Expansion joints let the slab GROW; contraction joints tell it WHERE to crack.** A contraction joint is a deliberate weakened plane — the slab will crack somewhere, and the joint decides where.

questions.stem: The size of an A1 drawing sheet is:
questions.solution:
**594 × 841 mm.**

The ISO A series is built on two rules: every sheet has an **aspect ratio of 1 : √2**, and each size is obtained by **halving the previous one across its longer side**. Because √2 is preserved under halving, the proportion never changes — which is why a drawing scales cleanly between sizes.

The series, starting from A0 whose area is exactly **1 m²**:

| Size | Dimensions (mm) | Area |
|---|---|---|
| **A0** | 841 × 1189 | 1 m² |
| **A1** | **594 × 841** | ½ m² |
| **A2** | 420 × 594 | ¼ m² |
| **A3** | 297 × 420 | ⅛ m² |
| **A4** | 210 × 297 | 1/16 m² |

Note the pattern that makes them easy to reconstruct: the **longer side of each sheet is the shorter side of the one above it**. So A1's 841 mm is A0's short side, A2's 594 mm is A1's short side, and so on. Knowing A0 = 841 × 1189 lets you derive the whole series, and option (a) is placed to catch anyone who names A0 when asked for A1.

**Margins and borders** on a drawing sheet (IS 10711):
- A **filing margin of 20 mm** on the left edge, for binding.
- A border of about 10 mm on the other three edges.
- A **title block** in the bottom right corner, of length 170 mm, carrying the title, drawing number, scale, projection method, date, and the names of the person who drew, checked and approved it.

Related drawing conventions examined alongside: **first angle projection** is the Indian and Nepali standard (third angle is American), and it is declared by a symbol in the title block. Recommended **scales** are 1:1, and reductions of 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200 and so on — the same decimal-and-halving pattern as the sheet sizes. **Line thicknesses** follow a √2 ratio too, and dimensions are always given in **millimetres** without repeating the unit.

examTip.trick: The A series halves each time: **A0 is 841 × 1189 mm (one square metre), and each subsequent size halves the longer dimension.** A1 = 594 × 841.
examTip.mnemonic: **A0 = 1 m², and every size has the same 1:√2 proportion** — which is why halving an A-sheet gives the next size with the same shape. A1 594×841, A2 420×594, A3 297×420, A4 210×297.

questions.stem: In PERT, the expected time of an activity is calculated as:
questions.solution:
**t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6.**

PERT treats each activity duration as uncertain and asks for three estimates:

| Estimate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **t_o** — optimistic | Shortest time if everything goes well |
| **t_m** — most likely | The modal duration, under normal conditions |
| **t_p** — pessimistic | Longest time if things go badly |

The durations are assumed to follow a **beta distribution**, whose mean is a weighted average giving the most likely value four times the weight of either extreme:

> **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6**

The variance of the activity is
> **σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

since for the beta distribution the range spans approximately six standard deviations.

Note that option (a), the plain arithmetic mean of the three, ignores the fact that the most likely duration is far better information than either extreme — which is precisely the point of the weighting.

**How the estimates are used.** The expected times give the critical path in the usual way. The variances of the activities **on that path** are then summed:
> σ_{project} = √(Σσ²)

and because the sum of many independent distributions tends to normal, the probability of finishing by any target date T follows from the standard normal deviate
> **Z = (T − T_e)/σ_{project}**

That probability statement is what PERT delivers and CPM cannot — a project manager can say "we have an 85% chance of finishing by June" rather than a single bare date.

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| Durations | **Deterministic**, one estimate | **Probabilistic**, three estimates |
| Orientation | **Activity**-oriented | **Event**-oriented |
| Suits | Repetitive work — construction | Novel work — research, development |
| Cost | Handles **time–cost trade-off (crashing)** | Time only, in its original form |

A known limitation: PERT considers the variance of the **critical path only**, so a near-critical path with high variance can overtake it and make the computed probability optimistic. Simulation methods address this.

examTip.trick: PERT's **beta distribution** weights the most likely time four times as heavily as the two extremes: **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Expected time (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6; standard deviation (t_p − t_o)/6; variance the square of that.** The key distinction from CPM: **PERT is probabilistic** (three time estimates, used for research and novel work), **CPM is deterministic** (one estimate, used for familiar construction) and adds **cost–time crashing**.

questions.stem: According to engineering codes of ethics, an engineer's paramount duty is to:
options: The client who pays the fee
The safety, health and welfare of the public
questions.solution:
**The safety, health and welfare of the public.**

This is the **fundamental canon** of every engineering code of ethics, and it is stated first precisely because it overrides everything else. The engineer's obligations to client, employer and profession are all real, but they are **subordinate** to public safety. Where they conflict, the public interest prevails.

The reason is the nature of the work. A structural failure, a contaminated water supply or a collapsed slope harms people who never chose to take the risk and could not have assessed it. Society grants engineers a licensed monopoly over such work, and the price of that privilege is that the profession polices itself in the public's favour.

The canons that follow from it, in the order they usually appear:

| Principle | Content |
|---|---|
| **Public safety paramount** | Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public above all |
| **Competence** | Perform services **only in areas of your competence** |
| Objectivity | Issue public statements that are objective and truthful |
| **Faithful agent** | Act faithfully for each employer or client, and **disclose all conflicts of interest** |
| Integrity | Avoid deceptive acts; no bribes, no secret commissions |
| Professional conduct | Conduct yourself honourably; **build reputation on merit**, not by injuring others |
| Continuing development | Maintain and update your competence; support the development of engineers under your supervision |

**In Nepal** this is given legal effect by the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055** and the Council's code of ethics. The Council may investigate professional misconduct and, in a serious case, **suspend or cancel registration** — which removes the right to practise.

The practical consequence, and the hardest part in real life: an engineer who finds that a design or a construction practice endangers the public is obliged to **report it and refuse to certify it**, even where that damages the client's interest, the employer's profit or the engineer's own position. That is what distinguishes a profession from a trade, and why the duty is stated as paramount rather than merely important.

examTip.trick: Every major engineering code of ethics places this **first and paramount** — above duty to the client, the employer, or the profession.
examTip.mnemonic: **Public safety, health and welfare come FIRST — above the client, above the employer.** That ordering is what makes it a profession rather than a trade, and it is what obliges an engineer to refuse or report unsafe work even when instructed otherwise.
